output:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing today announced the financial close of a loan of up to $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to help finance the restart of the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Linn County, Iowa.

WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) today announced the financial close of a loan of up to $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to help finance the restart of the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Linn County, Iowa. The investment will bring Iowa's only nuclear power plant back online, advancing President Trump's energy dominance agenda and Executive Order, Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base.

“President Trump has set an ambitious course to restore American nuclear leadership, and the restart of Duane Arnold Nuclear Plant in Iowa marks another step in advancing America’s nuclear renaissance,” said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly. “Returning 615 megawatts of reliable baseload generation will drive down electricity costs, while supporting thousands of American jobs. This Administration is pursuing a comprehensive nuclear strategy, restarting existing reactors, increasing the output of our nuclear fleet, and accelerating new construction, to build the abundant, affordable, and reliable power system required for American prosperity and reindustrialization.”

Duane Arnold’s restart will add 615 megawatts (MW) of reliable baseload power back on the grid—enough to power nearly 500,000 homes—and help meet growing electricity demand in Iowa and across the region. The project will create nearly 1,500 American jobs during construction and support more than 450 jobs during operations.

It is worth noting that the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) recently announced an investment exceeding $99 million for 21 selected projects aimed at promoting the development of geothermal energy throughout the United States. These projects are expected to conduct field-scale evaluations of advanced geothermal technologies, along with exploration drilling efforts designed to characterize and potentially confirm the presence of promising geothermal resources.

Furthermore, it can be suggested that the leadership of President Trump has played a role in advancing American geothermal innovation, which may unlock the significant domestic energy resources available in the nation. Geothermal energy has the potential to deliver reliable, continuous power, which can assist in meeting the increasing energy demand while also enhancing U.S. energy security.

Notably, DOE Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit remarked that these projects will provide opportunities for American innovators to tap into the expansive geothermal resources located beneath the surface. Under the guidance of President Trump, the advancement of next-generation geothermal technologies can lead to reduced costs, reinforce American energy dominance, and convert more of the abundant domestic geothermal resources into dependable and affordable energy.

In essence, the 21 selected projects will focus on enhancing geothermal development in two significant areas. Specifically, five of these projects will undertake field-scale tests of enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) to validate their technologies in practical settings, while 16 additional projects will engage in exploration drilling to identify and characterize next-generation geothermal resources that may hold promise. Collectively, these initiatives are expected to mitigate technical and development risks, as well as furnish essential information that can support future commercial projects and investments.

Ultimately, the data generated from these initiatives will be made publicly accessible through the DOE's Geothermal Data Repository (GDR), potentially providing industry professionals, researchers, and other stakeholders with valuable insights from the field tests and geothermal exploration activities. By making this information available, the projects may extend their benefits beyond individual sites, thereby aiding in the future development of technology and geothermal exploration across the industry. In summary, these efforts are anticipated to significantly contribute to the advancement of geothermal energy in the United States.
output:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced more than $99 million for 21 projects selected to advance geothermal energy development across the United States. The projects will conduct field-scale tests of next-generation geothermal technologies and exploration drilling to characterize and potentially confirm promising geothermal resources.

Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, the Energy Department is advancing American geothermal innovation to unlock the nation’s abundant domestic energy resources. Geothermal can provide reliable, around-the-clock power to help meet growing demand while strengthening U.S. energy security.

“These projects will empower American innovators to unlock the tremendous geothermal resources beneath our feet,” said DOE Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we’re advancing next-generation geothermal technologies that can lower costs, strengthen American energy dominance, and turn more of our vast domestic geothermal resources into reliable and affordable power.”

The 21 projects will advance geothermal development in two key areas. Five projects will conduct field-scale enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) tests to validate technologies under real-world conditions, while 16 additional projects will conduct exploration drilling to identify and characterize promising next-generation geothermal resources. Together, these efforts will help reduce technical and development risk and provide the information needed to support future commercial projects and investment.

Data generated by these projects will be publicly available through DOE’s Geothermal Data Repository (GDR), giving industry, researchers, and other stakeholders access to information from the field tests and geothermal exploration activities. Making these data available can extend the value of the projects beyond individual sites by helping inform future technology development and geothermal exploration across the industry.

It is a pleasure to be present with you today. Throughout my professional journey, I have had the opportunity to engage with issues that impact rural communities, particularly in relation to access to financial resources. My experiences at the Federal Reserve have further enhanced my understanding of both the opportunities and challenges faced by rural America, particularly as I have traveled extensively to various rural areas over the past several years.

Notably, these communities tend to encounter numerous difficulties, and they may also face unique obstacles that require adaptable solutions. What has particularly resonated with me is the degree of innovation and creativity that can often be observed in many of these solutions. It appears that we should actively seek to highlight these examples, disseminating successful practices and promoting ideas that may help expand opportunities and bolster economic growth throughout rural America.

For instance, in 2023, I had the chance to journey along the Blues Trail in the Mississippi Delta, traversing the route from Jackson to Memphis. Along this path, I engaged with local leaders and representatives from financial institutions, some of whom are here today, to gain insights into how once-thriving rural railroad towns are adjusting to both enduring and emerging challenges.

In Moorhead, Mississippi, which is often recognized as the location where the Southern crosses the Yellow Dog, I observed how a bank that had faced difficulties in maintaining its branch ultimately decided to donate its building to a community development financial institution, thereby preserving crucial access to banking services for a community that greatly requires this support.

Furthermore, in Clarksdale, Mississippi, I had the opportunity to visit the Travelers Hotel, which underwent redevelopment through the utilization of New Markets Tax Credits. This project now plays a significant role in the revitalization of the Blues tourism sector within that historic community. Overall, these experiences illustrate the importance of innovative approaches in addressing the challenges faced by rural communities.
output:
It is great to be here with you today. During my career, I've had the opportunity to work on issues affecting rural communities, especially access to capital. My time at the Federal Reserve has only deepened my appreciation for the opportunities and challenges of rural America, as I've traveled over the past several years to rural communities.

These communities share many challenges, and they also face distinct obstacles that require flexible solutions. What has stood out to me is the level of innovation and creativity behind many of those solutions. We should do more to elevate these examples, sharing what works and spreading ideas that can expand opportunity and support economic growth across rural America.

For example, in 2023, I had the opportunity to travel the Blues Trail in the Mississippi Delta, from Jackson to Memphis. Along the way, I met with local leaders and financial institutions, some of whom are represented here today, to learn how once-thriving rural railroad towns are adapting to both long-standing and emerging challenges.

In Moorhead, Mississippi, "where the Southern crosses the Yellow Dog,"2 I saw how a bank that had struggled to maintain a branch chose to donate its building to a community development financial institution (CDFI), preserving access to banking services for a community that needed it.

In Clarksdale, Mississippi, I visited the Travelers Hotel, which was redeveloped using New Markets Tax Credits and is now contributing to the resurgence of the Blues tourism industry in that historic community.

Huge congratulations to Michigan State University's James Madison College Class of 2025!1 It is an honor to speak to this inspiring and talented graduating class. Before I address the graduates, I would like to thank those who helped you get here: the parents, grandparents, siblings, aunts and uncles, friends, teachers, and mentors. Congratulations and thank you to all who lifted up the Class of 2025.

As a professor's kid and as an MSU professor, I have come to treasure commencements as important milestones. It is wonderful to be with you today. The flowers are starting to bloom in Beal Garden, the lawns around Beaumont Tower are turning the perfect shade of Spartan green, and the ducklings are making their appearance on the Red Cedar. After another chilly winter, campus is reaching peak beauty—just in time for you to leave Michigan State.

I am full of optimism about everything that lies ahead of you. Despite any sense of angst you may feel about moving on from Madison, I hope that you are filled with optimism, too. Spring is a time of new beginnings. You are ready for the next step. Today marks both the completion of a tremendous accomplishment, and an exciting new beginning. Some of you may be feeling uncertain. That is natural. Others of you may have detailed plans that you are ready to execute. Remember, if you keep your head down and your eyes fixed only on the map, you may miss unexpected opportunities. Life—like Michigan weather—is going to surprise you. As you leave here, I want you to remain optimistic and have confidence, because you are ready.

As proud graduates of James Madison University, it is essential to actively seek various avenues to contribute to the greater good throughout your lives. Engaging in public service can often be challenging, yet it consistently offers meaningful and deeply rewarding experiences. This engagement may take many forms, including working in education or government, conducting research to enhance our understanding, developing new technologies, volunteering for nonprofit organizations, or providing mentorship to junior colleagues. There are numerous ways, both substantial and minor, to contribute to the community. Thus, as you proceed through life, it is valuable to consider which paths will enable you to make a positive impact on society.

Ultimately, as graduates and members of the Spartan community, you are stepping into a world characterized by urgent needs and abundant opportunities. Over the course of my life, many of my proudest and most enriching memories were opportunities to serve. (Were any of you in 4-H like I was? Do you remember the pledge? It is "Head, Heart, Hands, and Health.") Heed your curiosity. Honor deep knowledge and thorough, persistent preparation. Embrace public service, however you define it.

Additionally, the Federal Open Market Committee reached a decision to revise its consensus statement following the completion of a public review process. Furthermore, this review process consisted of several key elements, including the hosting of Fed Listens events by Reserve Banks, the organization of a research conference by the Board, and the convening of policymaker discussions at FOMC meetings, which were supported by staff analysis. Notably, the changes implemented as a result of this review process tend to represent a logical progression, rather than a significant change in course, and are grounded in the committee's evolving understanding of the economy. Ultimately, the revisions made to the consensus statement appear to be a natural outcome of this review process.

In essence, the revised consensus statement underwent several adjustments, which may be viewed as an attempt to refine the committee's monetary policy strategy. Additionally, one of the key adjustments made to the consensus statement was the removal of language emphasizing the effective lower bound as a defining feature of the economic landscape. It is worth noting that this revision reflects a move away from the post-financial crisis era, and instead, the statement now emphasizes the importance of promoting maximum employment and stable prices across a broad range of economic conditions. Furthermore, this revision tends to make the committee's framework more robust, and can often be seen as a response to the changing economic environment.

It is worth noting that the previous framework review, which took place during 2019 and 2020, was conducted in a very different economic context, characterized by low growth, low inflation, and a flat Phillips curve. Notably, the overarching concern for central bankers at that time was how to operate in an environment where short-term interest rates were near the effective lower bound. However, today, the economic environment is very different, at least in part due to the economic consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic, which has brought about significant changes to the economic landscape. Ultimately, the revisions made to the consensus statement appear to be a necessary response to these changing circumstances, and tend to reflect the committee's ongoing effort to refine its monetary policy strategy. In summary, the Federal Open Market Committee's revised consensus statement represents a refinement of its monetary policy strategy, and appears to be a necessary response to the evolving economic environment.
output:
The FOMC revised its consensus statement after conducting a public review. That review consisted of three elements: first, Reserve Banks hosted Fed Listens events; second, the Board hosted a research conference; and third, we convened a series of policymaker discussions at FOMC meetings this year, supported by staff analysis. The changes implemented as a result of this review were a logical progression, not a change in course, grounded in our ever-evolving understanding of our economy. I will make note of four adjustments to the consensus statement and discuss each in turn.

First, the revised consensus statement removed language emphasizing the effective lower bound (ELB) as a defining feature of the economic landscape. Instead, it states that our monetary policy strategy is designed to promote maximum employment and stable prices across a broad range of economic conditions. This revision, reflecting a move away from the post–financial crisis era of historically low interest rates, makes our framework more robust. It is useful to recall that at the time of the FOMC's previous framework review, during 2019 and 2020, policymakers were considering an economy that had for many years demonstrated low growth, low inflation, and a very flat Phillips curve—meaning that inflation was not very responsive to slack in the economy. The overarching concern for central bankers at that time was how to operate when short-term interest rates are near the ELB. Today, of course, we are operating in a very different environment, at least in part brought on by the economic consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic.

output: Today the Fed communicates in a variety of ways, including policymaker speeches, Chair Powell's press conferences, and even through the Fed's social media channels. Clear and ample communication, however, has not always been the hallmark of the Fed. In the 1990s, cable news outlets would attempt to spot former Fed Chair Alan Greenspan walking into the building on the day of FOMC meetings. Commentators would pay careful attention to the size of his briefcase. The thought was that if the Chair was advocating a rate change, the briefcase would be bulging with documents to convince fellow policymakers. A light bag, on the contrary, would have signaled that a status quo policy decision was likely. Former Chair Greenspan seemed to value the element of surprise. In 1987, he famously quipped, "If I seem unduly clear to you, you must have misunderstood what I said."4 That said, during his tenure in later years, he initiated substantial changes in how Fed policymakers communicate with the public.

Building a Framework to Better Support Community Banks

Additionally, after acknowledging the significance of community banks and establishing a clear definition of these institutions, it is critical to identify the guiding principles that should govern their regulation and supervision. The principles that guide this approach are relatively simple and straightforward: the regulatory framework must be tailored to the associated risks, characterized by transparency, and consistently applied across similar institutions. In essence, the integration of these elements can create an opportunity to develop a sustainable regulatory and supervisory framework for community banks in the future.

Furthermore, this conference serves as an ideal platform to encourage discussions that may foster innovative ideas aimed at preserving the viability of community banking for the foreseeable future. While it would be unfeasible to provide an exhaustive plan for a community banking reform agenda within the confines of this speech, I recognize several opportunities that appear to be both promising and essential for consideration.

The Value of Experience 

Moreover, the process of constructing this framework for the future fundamentally begins with the personnel involved, specifically those who are responsible for making long-term decisions. It is essential to consider how we approach our responsibilities in this regard. We should emphasize successful examples from the past while also reflecting on the considerable amount of work that still lies ahead.

It is worth noting that Congress designated one seat on the Federal Reserve Board specifically for an individual who possesses demonstrated primary experience in either working within or supervising community banks. Although Congress did not specify any additional responsibilities linked to this particular seat on the Board, the establishment of this role serves as an implicit recognition of the value that such experience can contribute to the Board's various functions, particularly in the realm of bank regulation and supervision. In summary, the thoughtful integration of experience and principles can substantively enhance the regulatory environment for community banks.

It is worth noting that if any administration finds a way to remove Fed officials over policy differences, then future administrations will likely do so as well. Furthermore, the public would lose faith that the central bank will make decisions based only on what is best for all Americans. In essence, the credibility of the Fed would be lost as a result of such actions. Notably, that credibility enables the Fed to support a strong and stable economy for the benefit of American families and businesses. Our credibility has been built and sustained over many decades, and we have a duty to safeguard that priceless asset for our fellow citizens and for generations to come.

As Americans, we are motivated by the belief that freedom and democracy greatly enhance human fulfillment. The work to preserve and strengthen our own democracy can be noisy, frustrating, and, at times, embattled. Partisan political differences are normal, and indeed essential, in a thriving democracy. However, we ought to be united in our commitment to the higher principles that define our nation. Chief among them is respect for the rule of law. As John Adams wrote, ours is "a government of laws and not of men."

Furthermore, our public institutions carry us forward through change, and they embody our commitment to freedom, democracy, and service of the public good. The philosopher Edmund Burke warned that democratic institutions take much time, effort, and patience to build but can be torn down all too quickly. It is essential that we preserve what is good about these institutions, even as we strive to improve them.

While we will have political differences, at the end of the day, we all love this wonderful country, and want what is best for it and for our fellow Americans. Ultimately, these shared commitments and institutions remain essential to our continued success as a nation.

Furthermore, this objective can be achieved by establishing a distinct oversight program for community banks that is separate from those intended for larger and regional financial institutions, thereby allowing examiners to concentrate specifically on the risks and activities pertinent to small banks. This approach would also diminish the inclination to apply standards and expectations originally designed for larger, more complex institutions to community banks.

Additionally, in order to avoid ambiguity, it is beneficial to provide clarity regarding the identification of material financial risks within the supervisory process. This identification does not suggest an exclusive focus on merely checking compliance boxes while reviewing processes, procedures, and documentation, irrespective of the actual assessment of risk. Moreover, it does not imply neglecting other critical components of the established supervisory program.

As noted in the supervisory operating principles, an emphasis on material financial risks necessitates that examiners employ reasoned judgment in prioritizing issues throughout each phase of the examination process. This prioritization commences with the focus outlined in the pre-examination letter, continues through the scope of work during the examination, and involves distinguishing between findings that warrant formal attention and those that may be resolved through less formal avenues. The operating principles explicitly mention supervisory observations for matters that do not constitute violations but may still be documented in the examination report. Ultimately, this approach seeks to enhance the effectiveness of the supervisory process while ensuring that community banks are evaluated in a manner that is appropriate for their specific context.
output:
Community banks should be subject to strict supervisory oversight, but it must be commensurate with their smaller size, simpler business activities, and the modest risks they pose to U.S. financial stability. This could be accomplished by separating the community bank oversight program from those designed for larger and regional banks, focusing examiner attention on small bank risks and activities. This would also eliminate the temptation to "push down" standards and expectations to community banks, that were designed for larger and more complex institutions.

Material Financial Risk To avoid confusion, it may also be helpful to clarify what is meant by identifying material financial risks in the supervisory process. It does not mean focusing primarily on checking boxes in reviewing processes, procedures, and documentation, regardless of the assessment of risk. It also does not mean ignoring other aspects of the established supervisory program.

As the supervisory operating principles note, focusing on material financial risks requires examiners to use reasoned judgment to prioritize through every stage of an examination. This begins with targeting in the pre-examination letter, the examination's scope of work, and differentiating between findings that meet the threshold of a matter requiring attention, and those that can be addressed through less formal means. The operating principles specifically reference supervisory observations for those matters that do not rise to the level of a violation but may be included in an examination report.

PDFP has continued to increase at a solid pace so far in the third quarter, despite some further weakening in housing activity, as retail sales have shown further robust gains in July and August.

In the context of overseeing holding companies, it is important to note that the Federal Reserve is mandated by statute to depend "to the fullest extent possible" on the examinations conducted by the primary state or federal supervisors of subsidiary banks. In practice, this requirement can often impose considerable limitations on the supervisory activities of the Federal Reserve. This situation tends to apply to national banks that are regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as well as state non-member banks that fall under the purview of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and a state banking authority.

This statutory requirement is intended to minimize the potential for redundant and burdensome examination processes. Nevertheless, it is essential for the Federal Reserve to possess confidence in the supervisory processes and outcomes of the examinations conducted by the OCC, FDIC, and state banking agencies. Achieving this confidence typically necessitates access to and a comprehensive review of examination reports and related activities. In situations where reliance on such examinations is not feasible or where access to supporting documentation is unavailable, it may be necessary for the Federal Reserve to initiate its own review.

Furthermore, each bank examination culminates in the creation of a report of examination, which serves to document the findings of the examination. This report frequently includes supervisory observations or criticisms, as well as matters requiring attention (MRAs) or matters requiring immediate attention (MRIAs) when such issues are identified during the examination process. Additionally, the report contains the bank's supervisory ratings, which are determined according to the CAMELS rating system.

It is worth noting that the findings from examinations and the inclusion of specific matters within the report can have significant implications for the bank involved. Not only do they guide how banks prioritize their efforts to address identified issues, but the bank's CAMELS rating can also influence its eligibility for favorable treatment regarding banking applications, impact the cost of FDIC insurance premiums, affect the liquidity funding costs, and serve as an indicator of bank management performance for its board of directors. In conclusion, the intricate relationship between examination findings and their consequences highlights the importance of thorough oversight in maintaining the health of financial institutions.
output:
Reducing Overlap in Examinations In conducting holding company supervision, the Federal Reserve is required by statute to rely "to the fullest extent possible" on examinations performed by a subsidiary bank's primary state or federal supervisors. In practice, complying with this requirement imposes significant limits on the Fed's supervisory activities. This applies to national banks regulated by the OCC and state non-member banks regulated by the FDIC and a state banking regulator.

The requirement is designed to avoid redundant and burdensome examination processes. However, to be effective, the Fed must have confidence in the supervisory processes and outcomes of these OCC, FDIC, and state banking agency exams, which requires access to and a thorough review of examination reports and activities. Where it is not possible to rely on or we do not have access to an exam or supporting documentation of supervisory activity, we may need to conduct our own review.

Reports of Examination and Supervisory Ratings Each bank examination concludes with a report of examination. This report documents exam findings including any supervisory observations or criticisms, and matters requiring attention (MRAs) or matters requiring immediate attention (MRIAs), if any are found during the exam. The report also includes the bank's supervisory ratings according to the CAMELS rating system.

Exam findings and the inclusion of specific matters in the report can have serious consequences for the bank. In addition to directing how banks prioritize their efforts to remediate identified issues, the bank's CAMELS rating can influence whether the bank qualifies to receive favorable treatment of banking applications, affect the cost of FDIC insurance premiums, affect the cost of liquidity funding, and serve as an indication of bank management performance for its board of directors.

When the costs associated with running a bank increase, there tends to be a necessity for making adjustments if the institution hopes to sustain its profitability and, ultimately, its continued operation. This situation may often involve either reducing expenses or increasing fees for banking services.

Furthermore, it is worth considering how the realities of managing a business can inform our current regulatory approaches. This question becomes particularly significant when regulators contemplate the introduction of new or revised rules. Regulators may benefit from consistently evaluating three key areas: first, identifying the specific problem that the new regulation seeks to address; second, assessing the potential costs associated with this regulatory approach; and third, exploring alternative methods that might be available. Before delving into the proposed path forward, it is useful to present an example that illustrates this important concern.

Notably, the final regulations under the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) released in 2023 established new thresholds that categorize banks as "small," "intermediate," or "large." In this context, large banks are defined as those possessing more than $2 billion in assets. It appears that this rulemaking may have represented a missed opportunity to better align the CRA requirements with the realities faced by community banks, as it does not seem to recognize the fundamental distinctions among banks that operate with various balance sheets and business models. In essence, applying the same evaluation criteria to a bank with $2 billion in assets as to a bank with $2 trillion in assets may reflect an oversight regarding the essential differences among financial institutions, as well as the disproportionate costs that these regulations may impose on smaller banks.
output:
When a bank's costs increase, there is, by necessity, a need to make changes if the bank hopes to maintain profitability and ultimately its survival. This usually involves either cutting costs or raising prices on banking services.

How do the realities of operating a business inform our current approach to regulation? The question becomes acutely relevant when regulators consider imposing new or revised regulations. Regulators should always ask (1) what problem does this new regulation solve, (2) what are costs of this approach, and (3) are there alternative approaches? Before discussing the path forward, I would like to note an example that highlights this concern.

The final Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued in 2023 established new regulatory thresholds defining "small," "intermediate" and "large" banks, with the last category—large banks—including every bank with more than $2 billion in assets. In my view, this rulemaking represented a missed opportunity to rationalize the requirements of the CRA among community banks, and ignored the fundamental differences among banks with different balance sheets and business models. An approach that applies the same evaluation standards to a bank with $2 billion in assets as it does to a bank with $2 trillion in assets arguably represents a shortcoming in considering the fundamental differences among firms, and the disproportionate costs these standards may impose on the smallest banks.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that a scenario may arise in which inflation is at or below target, while employment appears to be near or higher than estimates of its maximum level, and the policy stance tends to be close to neutral or accommodative. Furthermore, the concept of maximum employment is not directly measurable and may evolve over time due to factors that are largely non-monetary in nature. Notably, changes to the underlying structure of the economy that are expected to persist in the longer run can often result in employment rising above existing assessments of maximum employment without necessarily generating upward pressure on inflation above 2 percent. Ultimately, the combination of low inflation and low unemployment may reflect positive supply shocks that are working their way through the economy, which can often lead to a situation in which the dual-mandate objectives may not necessarily be in tension. In essence, employment that appears stronger than its estimated maximum level may not require a policy response, as was the case during the second half of the 1990s, when the FOMC, under the leadership of then-Chairman Greenspan, reached a decision to hold off on rate increases even as unemployment moved below the estimated natural rates. Moreover, it is worth noting that strong productivity growth allowed for a combination of strong output growth and low and falling inflation, which tends to support the notion that the dual-mandate objectives can be achieved without being in conflict. It is also worth noting that this dynamic may be subject to variation, and the relationship between employment and inflation may be influenced by a range of factors. Ultimately, the challenge of balancing the maximum-employment and price-stability goals can often be complex, and may require a nuanced approach, as in the case where inflation is somewhat elevated, a weak or weakening labor market is experienced, and a policy stance that is already accommodative is in place, which may call for holding the policy rate at an accommodative level in order to achieve a balance between the dual-mandate objectives. In summary, the relationship between employment and inflation is complex, and may require a range of policy responses, depending on the specific circumstances, and ultimately, the goal of monetary policy is to achieve a balance between the maximum-employment and price-stability goals, which can often be challenging, but is essential for maintaining economic stability.
output:
Another example is when inflation is at or below target but employment seems near or higher than estimates of its maximum level and the policy stance is close to neutral or accommodative. As described in the FOMC's consensus statement, maximum employment is not directly measurable and evolves over time due to factors that are largely non-monetary. Changes to the underlying structure of the economy that are expected to persist in the longer run may result in employment rising above existing assessments of maximum employment without necessarily generating upward pressure on inflation above 2 percent. The combination of low inflation and low unemployment may reflect positive supply shocks that are working their way through the economy. In that case, absent price-stability risks, the dual-mandate objectives may not necessarily be in tension, and employment that appears stronger than its estimated maximum level may not require a policy response. This dynamic occurred during the second half of the 1990s, when then-Chairman Greenspan led the FOMC to hold off on rate increases even as unemployment moved below the estimated natural rates, as strong productivity growth allowed for a combination of strong output growth and low and falling inflation.

I will conclude this part of the discussion with an example of tension between our goals, with inflation somewhat elevated, a weak or weakening labor market, and a policy stance that is already accommodative. Under these conditions, balancing the maximum-employment and price-stability goals would call for holding the policy rate at an accommodative level.

It is worth noting that recent progress on efforts to lower inflation may have experienced a slowdown, as indicated by rising measures of Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation. Furthermore, on a year-over-year basis, total PCE inflation may have increased to 3.8 percent in April, largely driven by higher gasoline and fuel oil prices. Additionally, core PCE inflation appears to have risen further to 3.3 percent last month, marking a noticeable increase since September. However, other indicators of inflation, which tend to focus on the central tendency of price changes, including the trimmed mean PCE measure, suggest that core inflation may have adjusted closer to 2 percent since last September. It is also important to recognize that price pressures seem to have become increasingly concentrated within a limited range of goods categories, reflecting the effects of tariffs and unique changes in software pricing. When excluding these one-time factors, core PCE inflation may have remained only slightly above 2 percent, indicating a lack of pressures from the labor market and a degree of weakness in market rents.

In addition, it appears to be premature to fully evaluate the extent and duration of the economic impacts stemming from the ongoing conflict in Iran. I tend to maintain an optimistic outlook that, once the conflict is resolved, supply disruptions may lessen, leading to only a temporary effect on PCE inflation and minimal consequences for domestic economic activity. This perspective seems to align with current oil futures prices and the prevailing optimism within financial markets. However, if disruptions were to persist well into the latter part of the year, there may be broader implications for inflation that could emerge. In summary, while there are indications of rising inflation and potential economic impacts from external conflicts, the situation remains fluid and may evolve in various ways.
output:
Progress on lowering inflation appears to have stalled, with measures of PCE inflation moving up recently. On a 12-month basis, total PCE inflation picked up to 3.8 percent in April, mostly reflecting higher gasoline and fuel oil prices, and core PCE inflation rose further to 3.3 percent last month, up noticeably since September. However, other measures of inflation that focus on the central tendency of price changes, including the trimmed mean PCE measure, indicate that core inflation has moved down closer to 2 percent since last September. Price pressures have become increasingly concentrated in a few goods categories, reflecting tariff effects and idiosyncratic changes in software prices. After removing these one-off factors, core PCE inflation would have continued to hover only a bit above 2 percent, reflecting no pressures from the labor market and weakness in market rents.

It still seems early to assess the size and persistence of the economic effects from the Iran conflict. I am optimistic that, once the conflict is resolved, supply disruptions will ease, leaving a temporary imprint in PCE inflation and minimal impacts on domestic economic activity. This view seems consistent with oil futures prices and with financial market optimism. But, should disruptions persist well into the second half of the year, we could start to see broader effects on inflation.

Additionally, this process can often greatly benefit from increased interaction between federal regulators and their counterparts in state bank regulation. Furthermore, the importance of strengthening coordination between state regulators and the Federal Reserve is paramount. At a recent meeting of the Board's Subcommittee on Smaller Regional and Community Banking, my colleagues and I had the distinct pleasure of welcoming representatives from the Conference of State Bank Supervisors, which included four members of their State Bank Commissioner cohort. During this meeting, we gained first-hand insights into the successes, frustrations, concerns, and potential areas for improvement in the collaboration between state and federal regulators. Such direct conversations are invaluable, as they contribute significantly to building and enhancing these essential intergovernmental relationships.

Moreover, historically, one of the many commendable attributes of the Federal Reserve Board is its structural incentive to collaborate in order to achieve compromise. The governors operate under extended, staggered terms designed to shield them from the immediate influences of political considerations. The Board is composed of seven independent governors who frequently contribute their distinct perspectives on a variety of policy issues. While instances of dissent may attract considerable attention, the Federal Reserve has a long-standing tradition of engaging in thoughtful debates, exchanging views, and ultimately reaching more sustainable compromises on matters of rulemaking. The prevailing consensus on bank regulatory issues is not unexpected, as we work collectively toward the shared objectives of safety, soundness, and financial stability.
output:
While regulators tasked with implementing regulations, supervision, and guidance bear the ultimate responsibility for those policy choices, this process can greatly benefit from more interaction among federal regulators and our state bank regulatory counterparts. More extensive dialogue with state regulators can improve proposals in the formulation stage by sharing practical, real-world perspectives, including observations on the impacts of intended and unintended consequences. While it is challenging to anticipate the unintended consequences of reforms, casting a wide net for views can lead to better, less disruptive, and better-informed policy choices.

The importance of enhancing coordination between state regulators and the Federal Reserve cannot be overstated. At a recent meeting of the Board's Subcommittee on Smaller Regional and Community Banking, my colleagues and I were delighted to welcome representatives of the Conference of State Bank Supervisors and four of their State Bank Commissioner members. We learned firsthand about the successes, frustrations, concerns, and areas for improvement in the coordination between state and federal regulators. There is simply no substitute for these direct conversations and building upon and improving these important intergovernmental relationships.

Collaborative Approach to Reform Historically, one of the many virtues of the Federal Reserve Board is the structural incentive to work together to achieve compromise. Governors serve extended, staggered terms intended to insulate them from political considerations. The Board consists of seven independent governors who often bring their unique voices to a range of policy matters. While instances of dissent tend to attract the most attention, the Fed has a long history and tradition of engaging in thoughtful debate, exchange of views, and reaching more durable compromises on rulemaking matters. The history of consensus on bank regulatory matters is not surprising because we work toward common goals of safety and soundness and financial stability.

When I found myself in a position similar to yours, having recently graduated from Spelman College, I recall experiencing uncertainty regarding what the future may hold for me. I did not envision that I would eventually become a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors or even pursue a career as an economist, as I initially entered Spelman College as a major in physics and philosophy. It was only several years post-graduation, following an unanticipated encounter, that I began to view economics as a viable avenue for my career aspirations. At that particular time, I was furthering my studies in philosophy while residing in Senegal, and I encountered challenges in identifying the appropriate framework through which to investigate the significant questions that inspired and motivated me. Consequently, I made the decision to embark on an adventurous journey: hiking Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. Fortuitously, during this expedition, I encountered a British economist who, by the conclusion of my trek, persuaded me that economics possesses the necessary tools to engage with the questions I held in high regard. Within a few months, I returned to my home, enrolled in classes to prepare for a Ph.D. in economics, and commenced a trajectory that eventually led me to both Michigan State University and the Federal Reserve.

Today, as you prepare to leave the familiar environment of Case Hall and East Lansing, ready to embark on your next adventure, it is worth noting that I would like to present four guiding principles for you to consider as you navigate the journey that lies ahead: hope, curiosity, persistence, and a steadfast commitment to the principles of public service.
output:

I only came to see economics as a potential route several years after my graduation, following a chance encounter. It is worth noting that I expressed support for the Federal Open Market Committee's decision to maintain interest rates at our most recent policy meeting in March. Additionally, while economic growth has remained robust, there are early indications that it may be experiencing a slowdown. Labor market conditions have remained stable through February, and progress regarding inflation has eased; however, the overall outlook appears to be uncertain. These circumstances led me to advocate for maintaining the policy rate at what I consider a moderately restrictive level.

Furthermore, the long-term perspective illustrated by figure 9 indicates that the Federal Open Market Committee responded to the elevated inflationary environment following the pandemic by increasing the policy rate by 5.25 percentage points over a span of approximately 15 months, beginning in March 2022. After maintaining the rate at this restrictive level for more than a year, improvements in inflation allowed a reduction of the policy rate by a full percentage point last year, resulting in the current rate. The experience of inflation moderating toward the 2 percent target without a significant rise in unemployment has been historically unusual, but it is greatly welcomed.

In considering the future trajectory of policy, I intend to continuously evaluate incoming data, the developing economic outlook, and the balance of associated risks. Ultimately, it is important to emphasize that monetary policy does not follow a predetermined path. If economic conditions remain strong and inflation does not progress sustainably toward 2 percent, the present policy restraint may need to be preserved for an extended period. Conversely, should the labor market weaken unexpectedly or inflation decline more rapidly than anticipated, adjustments to policy may be warranted. In my assessment, there is no immediate necessity to expedite further changes to the policy rate. The current policy stance appears to be well positioned to address the risks and uncertainties inherent in fulfilling both aspects of our dual mandate.
output:
I supported the FOMC's decision to hold rates steady at our last policy meeting in March. Growth has remained solid so far but has started to show some signs of slowing. Labor market conditions have remained stable through February, and progress on inflation has eased, but the outlook is uncertain. These conditions led me to favor holding the policy rate constant at what I view as a moderately restrictive level.

The longer-term perspective provided by figure 9 shows that the FOMC responded to elevated inflation in the post-pandemic period by raising the policy rate 5-1/4 percentage points over about 15 months, starting in March 2022. After the Committee held the rate at that restrictive level for more than a year, progress on inflation allowed it to lower its policy rate by 1 full percentage point last year to its current level. The outcome of inflation moderating toward the 2 percent target without a large increase in unemployment was historically unusual but greatly welcomed.

Thinking about the future path of policy, I will continue to assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. As we emphasize, monetary policy is not on a preset course. If the economy remains strong and inflation does not continue to move sustainably toward 2 percent, the current policy restraint could be retained for longer. If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, policy could be eased accordingly. In my view, there is no need to be in a hurry to make further policy rate adjustments. The current policy stance is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

This passage serves as an introduction to the 2025 community banking research conference. It is worth noting that the speaker expresses regret about not being able to attend in person while also recognizing the significant contributions this conference has made in advancing research related to community banking and its associated issues.

Since its inception in 2013, the conference has effectively synthesized insights from academic research, regulatory bodies, and the banking sector, all aimed at deepening the understanding of the community bank business model. This effort is intended to better inform future policy decisions in the field.

Additionally, the speaker, who has served as the former Kansas state bank commissioner as well as a community banker, expresses appreciation for the conference's objectives. This year, the organizers have once again curated valuable research and developed a program featuring a broad array of perspectives that facilitate discussion and debate among participants.

Furthermore, ensuring the future and viability of the community banking sector remains a critical priority, particularly in light of the recent appointment of the speaker as Vice Chair for Supervision of the Federal Reserve Board by the President.

This particular role, established under the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, involves the responsibility to develop policy recommendations for the Board regarding the supervision and regulation of depository institution holding companies and other financial entities under its supervision. It also entails overseeing the regulatory compliance of these firms.

Ultimately, the speaker conveys an immense sense of honor and privilege in being entrusted with these significant responsibilities. The speaker looks forward to collaborating with stakeholders across the financial industry to modernize the regulatory and supervisory frameworks, which can foster continued economic growth and innovation within the banking system while enhancing the vital role of community banks.
output:
Welcome to the 2025 community banking research conference. While I regret that I cannot join you in person this year, I would like to take a moment to acknowledge the contributions this conference has made and continues to make in promoting research on community banking and related issues.

Since 2013, this conference has synthesized insights and perspectives from research and regulatory and banking communities with a single goal: deepening our understanding of the community bank business model in order to better inform future policy decisions.

As the former Kansas state bank commissioner and a community banker, I very much appreciate the goals of this conference. And again this year, the organizers have included valuable research and created a conference program that includes a wide range of perspectives that create an opportunity for discussion and debate.

Ensuring the future and viability of the community banking industry continues to be a top priority, especially as the President appointed me to serve as the Vice Chair for Supervision of the Federal Reserve Board.

This position, which was created under the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, requires the Vice Chair to "develop policy recommendations for the Board regarding supervision and regulation of depository institution holding companies and other financial firms supervised by the Board" and to also "oversee the supervision and regulation" of these firms.

It is an honor and an absolute privilege to be entrusted with these important responsibilities, and I look forward to working with all of our stakeholders in the financial industry to modernize supervision and regulation that allows for continued economic growth and innovation in the banking system and that enhances the critical role of community banks.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that the supervisory process may be subject to distractions from less relevant issues, which can often hinder its effectiveness. Furthermore, the prevalence of supervisory findings related to nonfinancial metrics tends to be driven by the time it may take to remediate certain issues, which can have a significant impact. Notably, this trend appears to be indicative of a shift in supervisory focus, one that moves beyond financial risk and toward non-financial risks and internal processes, and it is essential to evaluate whether this shift is appropriate. Ultimately, the diversity in business models, size, and geographic footprint among banks means that a uniform approach may not be suitable, and it is crucial to avoid forcing uniformity through comparative assessments. In essence, the supervisory findings made during the examination process have a significant impact on bank ratings, which can often have follow-on effects, such as limiting options for mergers and acquisitions activity, raising the cost of liquidity, or diverting resources away from other priorities. It is worth noting that guidance can also impose costs on banks, which may not always be obvious or quantified, and the purpose of guidance is to provide clarity and reduce implementation uncertainty and risk. Additionally, guidance must be clear, actionable, and account for the needs of the targeted firms, especially for community banks, in order to serve its purpose effectively. Ultimately, the effectiveness of the supervisory process and guidance depends on a careful consideration of these factors, and it is essential to reach a decision that balances the needs of all parties involved, which tends to be a complex and ongoing process that requires careful evaluation and consideration.
output:
In the supervisory process, we should guard against being distracted by less relevant issues. The prevalence of supervisory findings related to nonfinancial metrics is in part driven by the time it may take to remediate certain issues. However, we should also scrutinize whether this trend is indicative of our supervisory focus—beyond financial risk and toward non-financial risks and internal processes—and whether that shift is appropriate. We should also be aware that due to the vast diversity in business models, size, and geographic footprint among banks, we should not expect every firm to follow the same standards and must be careful to prevent forcing uniformity through "grading on a curve." This risk can be exacerbated through any type of horizontal-like reviews. The supervisory findings made during the examination process inform bank ratings, which can have follow-on effects like limiting options for mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity; raising the cost of liquidity; or diverting resources away from other, more important bank management priorities.

Guidance can also impose costs on banks that are not always obvious or quantified. The purpose of guidance is to provide clarity to banks and reduce implementation uncertainty and risk. To serve this purpose, however, guidance must be clear, actionable, and account for the needs of the targeted firms, especially for community banks.

Payroll employment growth may serve as an indicator of labor market momentum and can often help identify shifts in the path of the unemployment rate. When payroll gains are strong relative to trend labor force growth, they tend to point toward a lower unemployment rate and stronger labor market conditions, whereas weak payroll gains can often point toward a higher unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, because these data can be volatile or unreliable for a variety of reasons, closer attention tends to be paid to average payroll gains over a few months, which helps in understanding whether the labor market is moving closer to or further away from full employment.

Additionally, a multitude of other data is examined, both from the employment report and from other public and private surveys, in order to assess momentum and slack in the labor market. Regarding slack, data on discouraged and marginally attached workers and on involuntary part-time employment can indicate the extent of hidden unemployment and fragile employment. Furthermore, data on wage growth can help assess the relative strength of labor demand and supply, and the ratio of vacancies to unemployment also serves as a measure of labor market tightness. Regarding momentum, the composition of job gains by industry tends to indicate the breadth and depth of employment gains, and the payroll data are adjusted for persistent bias or expected revisions. Notably, indicators of layoffs, such as unemployment insurance claims, can detect early signs of a pickup in unemployment, and data on job openings also provide a signal about the strength of labor demand.

Regarding price stability, or inflation, the FOMC established 2 percent as the inflation goal in 2012, as measured by the annual change in the PCE price index. Consequently, policymakers closely monitor the recent path of total PCE inflation and how it is expected to evolve going forward. Ultimately, these various indicators together provide a broad framework for assessing labor market conditions and the outlook for inflation.
output:

Of course, I look at a multitude of other data, both from the employment report and other public and private surveys, to assess momentum and slack in the labor market. input:
Additionally, community banks, in a manner similar to all banking institutions, are frequently required to obtain regulatory approval in order to engage in certain business activities and mergers, or to undertake new activities. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the process of applying for such regulatory approval appears to have become uncertain, cumbersome, disruptive, and slow in recent years.

Moreover, in some instances, application forms may fail to require a bank to submit the necessary information that is needed in order to evaluate an application properly. Additionally, the application process can often include standards that appear to make little sense when they are applied to community banks, such as the use of restrictive screens for evaluating the competitive effects of mergers in rural and underserved communities.

Furthermore, the process tends to lack specific action timelines that are necessary for business planning purposes. It is worth noting that mergers and acquisitions involve the coordination of a number of time-dependent processes, including transaction closing and staffing related planning, as well as the process of scheduling technology integrations with specialized vendors. In essence, the missing of deadlines can often be costly for the institutions involved, and we are currently working to improve this process by addressing these and other challenges, especially for community banks.

Additionally, I would like to discuss transparency, which I view as a critical element of the regulatory and supervisory processes. Furthermore, transparency in supervisory expectations appears to be just as important as transparency in regulatory requirements, and yet it often tends to receive the least scrutiny and attention.

Moreover, in part, the lack of transparency for supervision may result from information security rules and the manner in which they apply to communication between banks and examiners. It is worth noting that these have been protected from public scrutiny under the broad categorization of confidential supervisory information (CSI). Ultimately, the labeling of information as CSI tends to result in significant restrictions on its disclosure, and banks and bank employees may be subject to criminal penalties if they disclose CSI without regulatory approval, even if doing so would serve beneficial purposes for bank safety and soundness.
output:
Like all banks, community banks often require regulatory approval to engage in some business activities and mergers, or to engage in new activities. The process of applying for regulatory approval has become uncertain, cumbersome, disruptive, and slow.

In some cases, application forms may not require a bank to submit the necessary information needed to evaluate an application. The application process may also include standards that make little sense when applied to community banks, like using restrictive screens for evaluating the competitive effects of mergers in rural and underserved communities.

In addition, the process often lacks specific action timelines necessary for business planning purposes. Mergers and acquisitions involve coordinating a number of time-dependent processes, including transaction closing and staffing related planning, and the process of scheduling technology integrations with specialized vendors. Missing deadlines can be costly for the institutions involved, and we are currently working to improve this process by addressing these and other challenges, especially for community banks.

Transparency Finally, I would like to discuss transparency, which I see as a critical element of the regulatory and supervisory processes. Transparency in supervisory expectations is just as important as transparency in regulatory requirements, and yet it often receives the least scrutiny and attention.

In part, the lack of transparency for supervision results from information security rules and how they apply to communication between banks and examiners. These have been protected from public scrutiny under the broad categorization of "confidential supervisory information" (CSI). Labeling information as CSI results in significant restrictions on its disclosure—banks and bank employees are subject to criminal penalties if they disclose CSI without regulatory approval even if doing so would serve beneficial purposes for bank safety and soundness.

output:
During his stay on the station, Menon will conduct scientific research and technology demonstrations aimed at advancing human space exploration and benefiting life on Earth. In September 2023, when NASA’s Perseverance rover arrived at the inner edge of Mars’ Jezero Crater, mission scientists experienced surprise regarding their discoveries. This geologic area, referred to as the “Margin Unit,” extends along the ancient shoreline of a Martian lake. The scientists anticipated the presence of sedimentary rocks, which typically form as layers of sand accumulate over extended periods. It is worth noting that sedimentary rocks on Earth, which consist of clay and silt, tend to preserve evidence of past microbial life effectively. Furthermore, the scientists expressed particular interest in the strong signals of carbonate minerals that had been detected by Mars orbiters, as these minerals frequently form in environments on Earth that can support life, such as shallow oceans and lakes.

Contrary to their expectations, the rover team identified igneous rock, which can form either from magma located deep underground or from volcanic activity at the surface. Igneous rocks serve as exceptional record-keepers due to the presence of mineral crystals that encapsulate details about their formation. This situation allowed for the preservation of a remarkably intricate record of water activity on early Mars. Notably, the rocks demonstrated evidence of having interacted with water on at least three distinct occasions, with each event contributing to changes in their chemistry and physical appearance. The results of these findings were published on a Monday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

Additionally, the instrument responsible for these findings is known as SuperCam, which is situated on the rover’s mast. This instrument determines the mineralogical composition of geologic features based on the light they reflect. When the science team identifies a rock of interest, they can issue commands for SuperCam to project its laser at distances of up to 21 feet (6.5 meters). The spectrum produced by the resulting plasma provides insights into the target’s chemical composition. To date, Perseverance has conducted analyses of more than 185 bedrock targets within this unit using this method. Ultimately, these insights contribute to a deeper understanding of Mars' geological history and potential habitability.

“Before we arrived at the Margin Unit, the main hypothesis — derived from orbital observations — was that the carbonate seen from orbit formed from interaction with the lake that existed in Jezero Crater,” said Candice Bedford, a research scientist at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana, and the study’s lead author. “But now we know that this location became a sort of crossroads for aqueous systems. The Margin Unit findings are important because Jezero Crater sits inside one of the largest exposures of carbonate on Mars, so what we learn here reaches well beyond this crater.”

Perseverance explored the Margin Unit across approximately 870 feet (265 meters) of elevation. At higher elevations, it found rock that was coarse-grained and crystalline — hallmarks of the mineral olivine — with almost no sign that water had ever touched it. Made of magnesium and iron, the area’s olivine unit formed in a body of magma deep underground, cooling slowly enough for its grains to grow large, and reached the surface only after the ground above it eroded away. Lower in the unit, on the lakebed, the rock looks transformed, as the olivine grains were fractured with silica between them.

Carbonate and silica minerals are an important signpost in the search for ancient life. When water interacts with olivine on Earth, the reaction can release hydrogen, which can be a food source for some microbes, and it leaves behind carbonate and silica, two minerals that lock in traces of the past existence of those microbes.

The Perseverance team can determine the sequence of the Margin Unit’s interactions with water, but not their age. On the first occasion water reached the rocks of the Margin Unit, carbon-dioxide-rich groundwater reacted with olivine, resulting in ridges of carbonate that run through the fractures in bedrock at low elevations. Today, these carbonate-filled fractures are left standing as the softer rock around them wears away.

“Some of the Margin Unit rocks also contain silica,” said Eleni Ravanis, a planetary scientist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa and a coauthor of the study. “Turning olivine into carbonate can leave silica behind, and we see more of that silica in rocks that sat below the water line.”

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was established by Congress in 1969 to acknowledge astronauts who have distinguished themselves through exceptional bravery and meritorious contributions to the well-being of both the nation and humanity. Since the inception of the space program, a total of 34 individuals have been awarded this honor, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia, who received the recognition posthumously. 

It is worth noting that NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that under President Trump’s guidance, America has been positioned to regain its leadership in the global space sector. This has been demonstrated through initiatives such as the Artemis program, which has provided NASA with the necessary resources and direction to compete in the current space race. Furthermore, he highlighted the extraordinary skill and bravery exhibited by the Artemis II crew, showcasing what American leadership and exploration can achieve at their best. This accomplishment was facilitated by the exemplary efforts of the NASA workforce, in conjunction with industry collaborators and international partners, illustrating the potential for significant achievements when there is a commitment to ambitious objectives. 

Ultimately, the first crewed mission of NASA’s Artemis program has set the stage for the planned Artemis III test flight in 2027, which aims to validate rendezvous and docking capabilities between the Orion spacecraft and commercial human landing systems. This will be followed by the Artemis IV mission in 2028, which is intended to return American astronauts to the lunar surface, marking a significant milestone in ongoing space exploration efforts. Overall, these initiatives emphasize a renewed focus on exploring and establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.
output:
The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was authorized by Congress in 1969 to recognize an astronaut who in the performance of duties has distinguished himself or herself by exceptionally brave and meritorious efforts, and contributions to the welfare of the nation and humanity. There now are 34 recipients of the award since the beginning of the space program, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia who received the award posthumously.

“President Trump’s leadership has put America back on a path to lead the world in space, from creating the Artemis program to giving NASA the resources and mandate to win this new space race,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The Artemis II crew answered that call with extraordinary skill and courage, showing the world the Moon again and what American leadership and exploration look like at their best. Their achievement was made possible by the exceptional NASA workforce, alongside our industry and international partners, who showed once again what can be accomplished when we commit to big, bold endeavors. We will build on this success as we return to the lunar surface and establish an enduring presence on the Moon.”

The first crewed mission under NASA’s Artemis program paved the way for the 2027 Artemis III test flight in low Earth orbit to demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems, and the Artemis IV mission in 2028, which will return American astronauts to the lunar surface.

input: NASA astronaut Anil Menon, together with Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, arrived safely at the International Space Station on Tuesday. This arrival brings the crew of the orbiting laboratory to a total of 10 individuals for approximately the next two weeks. The trio launched aboard the Soyuz MS-29 spacecraft at 10:47 a.m. EDT, which corresponds to 7:47 p.m. local time, from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. After a journey lasting three hours and encompassing two orbits, the spacecraft docked at 1:52 p.m. with the station's Prichal module. Following the opening of the hatch, which is expected at about 4 p.m., the new arrivals will be welcomed by the space station Expedition 74 crew. This crew includes NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams, along with ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov, Sergei Mikaev, and Andrey Fedyaev. NASA's live coverage of the hatch opening is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. on NASA+, Amazon Prime, and YouTube. It is worth noting that individuals can learn how to watch NASA content through a variety of online platforms, including social media. During his stay aboard the station, Menon will conduct scientific research and technology demonstrations aimed at advancing human space exploration and benefiting life on Earth. He will continue research to refine in-space production of semiconductor crystals, which may enable the large-scale manufacturing of components needed for high-performance computers, artificial intelligence, and improved medical devices. Additionally, Menon will perform ultrasound using augmented reality and artificial intelligence methods that could eliminate the need for medical support from Earth on future space missions. He will serve as a test subject helping researchers understand how blood flow is affected in space to protect future astronauts. Furthermore, he will test bioprinting vascular constructs in microgravity to improve understanding of the aging process to advance therapeutic developments. Expedition 75 is scheduled to begin on Sunday, July 26, following the departure of Williams, Kud-Sverchkov, and Mikaev, as they conclude an eight-month science mission aboard the orbital outpost. Ultimately, this highlights the continuous rotation of crews and the ongoing scientific work on the station.
output:

Following hatch opening, expected about 4 p.m., the new arrivals will be welcomed by the space station Expedition 74 crew: NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams; ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot; and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov, Sergei Mikaev, and Andrey Fedyaev.

NASA’s live coverage of hatch opening begins at 3:30 p.m. on NASA+, Amazon Prime, and YouTube. Learn how to watch NASA content through a variety of online platforms, including social media.

During his stay aboard the station, Menon will conduct scientific research and technology demonstrations aimed at advancing human space exploration and benefiting life on Earth. He will continue research to refine in-space production of semiconductor crystals to enable the large-scale manufacturing of components needed for high-performance computers, artificial intelligence, and improved medical devices. Menon also will perform ultrasound using augmented reality and artificial intelligence methods that could eliminate the need for medical support from Earth on future space missions. He will be a test subject helping researchers understand how blood flow is affected in space to protect future astronauts. He also will test bioprinting vascular constructs in microgravity to improve understanding of the aging process to advance therapeutic developments.

Expedition 75 is scheduled to begin on Sunday, July 26, following the departure of Williams, Kud-Sverchkov, and Mikaev, as they conclude an eight-month science mission aboard the orbital outpost.

output:
Laurie E. Locascio, under secretary of commerce for standards and technology and director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), has been elected to the National Academy of Engineering — one of the highest professional distinctions accorded to an engineer.

Locascio leads NIST’s collaborative efforts with industry, academia and government to unleash U.S. innovation by advancing technology, measurements and standards. A key priority for her is the successful implementation of the CHIPS for America initiative, a $50 billion suite of programs to strengthen and revitalize U.S. leadership in semiconductor research, development and manufacturing.

In addition, Locascio is working to advance and grow NIST’s work in critical emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum information science, cybersecurity and privacy, biotechnology, energy and advanced communications. She also promotes NIST’s continuing role in advancing federal and international standards, which helps ensure U.S. economic competitiveness and technology leadership.

Before being confirmed as NIST director in April 2022, Locascio served as vice president for research at the University of Maryland College Park and University of Maryland Baltimore. Prior to that, she worked at NIST for 31 years, starting as a research biomedical engineer and rising to lead the agency’s Material Measurement Laboratory. She also served as the acting associate director for laboratory programs, the No. 2 position at NIST, providing direction and operational guidance for NIST’s research programs.

Locascio has published 115 scientific papers and has received 12 patents in the fields of bioengineering and analytical chemistry. She is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Chemical Society, the American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering, and the National Academy of Inventors.

Biden signed an Executive Order (EO) to build U.S. capacity to evaluate and mitigate the risks of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to ensure safety, security, and trust, while promoting an innovative, competitive AI ecosystem that supports workers and protects consumers.
