Additionally, it is worth noting that the electric field in close proximity to a membrane in a solution that is similar to the human body can exhibit considerable strength, as Hoogerheide reached a decision to emphasize. Furthermore, the strength of this field tends to experience a decline with increasing distance, thereby creating substantial field gradients that may repel nearby particles, a phenomenon that the researchers figured might occur. Ultimately, the team decided to utilize neutron beams to investigate this phenomenon in greater detail.

Notably, neutrons are capable of distinguishing between different isotopes of hydrogen, and the research team designed experiments that explored the effect of a membrane on nearby molecules of a polymer known as PEG, which forms chargeless nano-sized particles. In essence, hydrogen is a major constituent of PEG, and by immersing the membrane and PEG into a solution of heavy water, which is composed of deuterium in place of ordinary water's hydrogen atoms, the team was able to measure the proximity of the PEG particles to the membrane. Moreover, the researchers employed a technique known as neutron reflectometry, as well as instruments at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, to conduct their experiments.

It is worth noting that the combination of these experiments and molecular dynamics simulations revealed evidence that suggests the membranes' powerful field gradients may be the primary cause of the repulsion, with the PEG molecules experiencing stronger repulsion from charged surfaces than from neutral surfaces. Additionally, the findings appear to demonstrate that well-known physics can manifest in unexpected contexts, which may encourage scientists to investigate this phenomenon further. Furthermore, the research tends to indicate that the understanding of interactions at the nanoscale may need to be revised to incorporate this newly observed phenomenon.

Moreover, the research has been documented in a paper authored by M. Aguilella-Arzo, D.P. Hoogerheide, M. Doucet, H. Wang, and V.M. Aguilella, titled "Charged biological membranes repel large neutral molecules by surface dielectrophoresis and counterion pressure," which was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. Ultimately, the study tends to contribute to our understanding of the complex interactions that occur at the nanoscale, and it is likely that this research will have significant implications for future studies in this field.

“The electric field right near a membrane in a salty solution like our bodies produce can be astoundingly strong,” Hoogerheide said. “Its strength falls off rapidly with distance, creating large field gradients that we figured might repel nearby particles. So we used neutron beams to look into it.”

Neutrons can distinguish between different isotopes of hydrogen, and the team designed experiments that explored a membrane’s effect on nearby molecules of PEG, a polymer that forms chargeless nano-sized particles. Hydrogen is a major constituent of PEG, and by immersing the membrane and PEG into a solution of heavy water — which is made with deuterium in place of ordinary water’s hydrogen atoms — the team could measure how closely the PEG particles approached the membrane. They used a technique known as neutron reflectometry at the NCNR as well as instruments at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Together with molecular dynamics simulations, the experiments revealed the first-ever evidence that the membranes’ powerful field gradients were the culprit behind the repulsion: The PEG molecules were more strongly repelled from charged surfaces than from neutral surfaces.

While the findings do not reveal any fundamentally new physics, Hoogerheide said, they do show well-known physics in an unexpected place, and that should encourage scientists to take notice — and explore it further.

“We need to add this to our understanding of how things interact at the nanoscale,” he said. “We’ve demonstrated the strength and significance of this interaction. Now we need to investigate how it affects these crowded environments where so much biology happens.”

Notably, a group within the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium, led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Johns Hopkins University, and the University of California, Davis, has conducted a study to test the full genome's ability to support the sequencing of DNA from thousands of people. It is worth noting that the findings of this study may have a profound impact on research into genetic disorders.

Furthermore, this template tends to provide a framework for guiding the assembly of the DNA strings in the correct order. It is worth noting that this process can often be complex and may require careful analysis.

output:
Alongside the newly updated human genome, which fills in long-standing gaps to fully spell out the more than 3 billion letters that compose our genetic code, a separate companion study has shown it can serve as an accurate template that improves our DNA sequencing capabilities by leaps and bounds.

A group within the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium — the initiative that completed the genome — led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Johns Hopkins University and the University of California, Davis, tested the full genome’s ability to support the sequencing of DNA from thousands of people. In a new paper published in the journal Science, the researchers found that it corrected tens of thousands of errors produced by the previous rendition of the genome and was better for the analysis of more than 200 genes of medical relevance. The findings suggest that the T2T’s genome could greatly propel research into genetic disorders, and that further in the future, patients might reap the benefits of more reliable diagnoses.

When clinicians and researchers sequence DNA to study or diagnose a genetic disorder, they use machines that produce strings of DNA, each mirroring a section of a patient’s or research subject’s genome. Then they compare those strings to a template, called a reference genome, to get an idea of what order to place them in.

“If sequencing DNA is like putting together a puzzle, then the reference genome is like the picture of the finished puzzle on the box. It helps guide you in putting together the pieces,” said NIST biomedical engineer Justin Zook, a co-author of the study.

At those centers, workers engage in the sorting of clothing by utilizing handheld devices that emit near-infrared light. These devices are capable of measuring the extent to which the light either passes through or scatters off the fabric, thereby generating a distinctive pattern that functions as a sort of fingerprint. This unique identifier can be instrumental in recognizing the types of fibers present in the clothing. This process, known as near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, also finds application in automated conveyor belt systems; however, it is important to note that current techniques still necessitate substantial manual labor.

In recent years, manufacturers of recycling equipment have increasingly integrated machine learning and artificial intelligence into the enhancement of their sorting algorithms. In order to effectively train these algorithms, high-quality reference data is essential.

This is where the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) database becomes significant. This database, referred to as the Near-Infrared Spectra of Origin-defined and Real-world Textiles, or NIR-SORT, encompasses 64 distinct types of fabric along with the corresponding NIR fingerprints they yield. The database includes pure fiber types such as cotton and polyester, blended fiber types such as spandex blends, and real-world fabrics sourced from thrift stores. Manufacturers of NIR scanner systems can utilize this database to train and evaluate their sorting algorithms, thereby enhancing the performance of their products.

Notably, challenges arise when fibers exhibit similarities, such as cotton and hemp, leading to comparable near-infrared signals. The same issue applies to cotton and polyester blends, raising the question of whether a given sample is a new fiber or a blend of two or more fibers. Katarina Goodge, a NIST research chemist who spearheaded the development of the database, emphasizes that artificial intelligence has the potential to refine the decision-making process, thereby increasing accuracy.

Given that NIST serves as the nation’s measurement institute, it possesses both the equipment and the expertise necessary to populate this database with exceptionally high-quality spectral data. This advancement may lead to a reduction in errors associated with fabric identification, ultimately facilitating a greater volume of textiles being recycled. In summary, the integration of this sophisticated database and advanced technology appears to signify a promising step forward for the textile recycling industry.

Additionally, it is worth noting that the synthesis of DNA sequences, which are part of computers known as strand displacement circuits, tends to occur separately and in a double-stranded form, in order to prevent undesired binding. Furthermore, this double-stranded form can often act as a locked gate, which may only unlock if the target sequence comes along and takes the place of one of the strands, thereby reaching a state of binding. Notably, the double strand is characterized by the fact that every chemical base on each strand is bound to a base on the other, which appears to be a crucial aspect of its function.

In essence, the researchers, including Schaffter and Elizabeth Strychalski, leader of NIST's Cellular Engineering Group and co-author of the study, reached a decision to mimic this locked gate function in their RNA circuit, keeping in mind that cells would ultimately have to produce these locked gates themselves. It is worth noting that the researchers wrote the sequences in such a way that one half of the strands could bind with the other half, which tends to result in the RNA sequences folding on themselves, thereby ensuring they are in a locked state. Ultimately, the binding process can often lead to the formation of a locked gate, which may be an important aspect of the circuit's function.

Furthermore, the gates would need to be composed of two chemically bound but distinct strands, which appears to be a necessary condition for their proper functioning. Additionally, the team obtained the double-stranded design in their gates by incorporating a stretch of RNA called a ribozyme near the folding point of the gates, which tends to sever itself after the RNA strand it was embedded in folded, resulting in the creation of two separate strands. In summary, the researchers developed a method to create locked gates in RNA circuits, which may have important implications for the field, and ultimately, the development of these gates tends to depend on the careful design of the RNA sequences and the incorporation of specific elements, such as ribozymes.
output:
To prevent undesired binding, DNA sequences that are part of computers known as strand displacement circuits are usually synthesized (in machines rather than cells) separately and in a double-stranded form. With every chemical base on each strand bound to a base on the other, this double strand acts as a locked gate that would only unlock if the target sequence came along and took the place of one of the strands.

Schaffter and Elizabeth Strychalski, leader of NIST’s Cellular Engineering Group and co-author of the study, sought to mimic this “locked gate” function in their RNA circuit, keeping in mind that, ultimately, cells would have to produce these locked gates themselves. To set cells up for success, the researchers wrote the sequences so that one half of the strands could bind flush with the other half. Binding this way, RNA sequences would fold on themselves like a hotdog bun, ensuring they are in a locked state.

But to work properly, the gates would need to be two chemically bound but distinct strands, more like a hamburger bun or sandwich than a hotdog bun. The team obtained the double-stranded design in their gates by coding in a stretch of RNA called a ribozyme near the folding point of the gates. This particular ribozyme — taken from the genome of a hepatitis virus — would sever itself after the RNA strand it was embedded in folded, creating two separate strands.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology, which operates within the United States Department of Commerce, has reached a decision to award cooperative agreements of up to 1.5 million dollars to two organizations. These agreements are intended to support the creation of curricula and programs that will provide training in standards implementation for both the current and future regenerative medicine workforce. It is worth noting that the recipients of these awards were identified through an open and competitive process that was announced earlier in the year.

Regenerative medicine, which can often be understood to encompass cell therapy, gene therapy, and therapeutic tissue engineering, appears to aim at harnessing the body's innate capacity for healing in order to regenerate and replace damaged or diseased cells, tissues, and organs. Furthermore, this field may offer unprecedented potential for the treatment of previously intractable diseases, such as cancer and genetic disorders.

Sheng Lin-Gibson, who serves as chief of the Biosystems and Biomaterials Division at NIST, stated that the agency was thrilled to announce these new partnerships for the development of an innovative standards education program. This program is expected to pave the way for flexible and immersive learning experiences that support advanced biomanufacturing. Additionally, these educational programs are intended to facilitate the adoption of standards and best practices, which can often increase the quality and consistency of advanced therapies and ultimately may contribute to a reduction in costs.

The organizations that will receive these awards are Brammer Bio, which is a part of Thermo Fisher Scientific's Patheon Pharma Services, and the Standards Coordinating Body for Gene, Cell and Regenerative Medicines and Cell-Based Drug Discovery, which is a nonprofit organization based in Gaithersburg, Maryland. These organizations will produce a wide range of training opportunities, and these opportunities tend to include traditional classroom and hands-on teaching, self-paced e-learning, and the use of digital tools, multimedia resources, and immersive augmented reality. Ultimately, this initiative appears to represent a coordinated effort to strengthen standards implementation across the regenerative medicine workforce.
output:

Researchers may have not yet fully mastered the additive manufacturing process, commonly referred to as 3D printing, of metals. Gaps in the understanding of the internal dynamics of metal during this process have resulted in inconsistent outcomes. However, a recent breakthrough has the potential to provide an unprecedented level of control over metal 3D printing.

Utilizing two distinct particle accelerator facilities, scientists from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden, and various other institutions have conducted an in-depth examination of the internal structure of steel during the melting and solidifying phases of 3D printing. The results of their research, published in the journal Acta Materialia, introduce a computational tool that can significantly enhance the predictive and controlling capabilities of 3D-printing professionals regarding the characteristics of printed components. This advancement may improve the consistency and overall feasibility of this technology for large-scale manufacturing applications.

A prevalent technique for fabricating metal components involves the sequential welding of powdered metal using lasers, layer by layer, to achieve a specified shape. In the initial phases of printing with a metal alloy, the material experiences rapid heating and cooling, causing its atoms, which can consist of various elements, to form ordered, crystalline structures. These crystals play a critical role in determining essential properties, such as toughness and corrosion resistance, of the finished part. Different crystal structures can develop, each exhibiting unique advantages and disadvantages.

It is worth noting that, according to NIST physicist Fan Zhang, who co-authored the study, controlling the microstructure during the initial stages of the printing process may lead to the formation of desired crystals and ultimately dictate the performance of additively manufactured components.

Although the printing process tends to minimize material waste and enables the production of more complex shapes compared to traditional manufacturing methods, researchers continue to encounter challenges in guiding metal toward specific types of crystal structures. In summary, the advancements presented in this research may pave the way for improved consistency and functionality in metal 3D printing.
output:
Researchers have not yet gotten the additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, of metals down to a science completely. Gaps in our understanding of what happens within metal during the process have made results inconsistent. But a new breakthrough could grant an unprecedented level of mastery over metal 3D printing.

Using two different particle accelerator facilities, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden and other institutions have peered into the internal structure of steel as it was melted and then solidified during 3D printing. The findings, published in Acta Materialia, unlock a computational tool for 3D-printing professionals, offering them a greater ability to predict and control the characteristics of printed parts, potentially improving the technology’s consistency and feasibility for large-scale manufacturing.

A common approach for printing metal pieces involves essentially welding pools of powdered metal with lasers, layer by layer, into a desired shape. During the first steps of printing with a metal alloy, wherein the material rapidly heats up and cools off, its atoms — which can be a smattering of different elements — pack into ordered, crystalline formations. The crystals determine the properties, such as toughness and corrosion resistance, of the printed part. Different crystal structures can emerge, each with their own pros and cons.

“Basically, if we can control the microstructure during the initial steps of the printing process, then we can obtain the desired crystals and, ultimately, determine the performance of additively manufactured parts,” said NIST physicist Fan Zhang, a study co-author.

While the printing process wastes less material and can be used to produce more complicated shapes than traditional manufacturing methods, researchers have struggled to grasp how to steer metal toward particular kinds of crystals over others.

Too many inadequate or misleading reports can prompt a sort of “gold rush” mentality similar to what occurred in the late 1990s and early 2000s with a then-emerging technology: carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Based on wildly enthusiastic early reports, many believed they would become the successor to silicon semiconductor elements in microelectronics. But when initial claims proved overstated, interest dried up along with funding.

“CNTs are a hugely instructive example,” Franklin said. “So much hype and overstated claims led to disillusionment and frustration rather than steady, collaborative and accurate progress. After a frenzy of activity, the eventual distaste resulted in a massive shift of research funding and attention going to other materials. It has taken a decade to bring deserved attention back to CNTs, and even then many feel it is not enough.”

Uniform benchmarking and reporting can minimize those sorts of convulsive effects and help scientists convince the research community that they have made genuine progress. “By using these guidelines,” the authors conclude, “it should be possible to comprehensively and consistently reveal, highlight, discuss, compare, and evaluate device performance."

Following this, the researchers would undertake a comparison of the data with the predictions of a widely used computational model that was developed in the ’80s and that describes the solidification of alloys. Within the synchrotrons, the authors set up additive manufacturing conditions for hot-work tool steel, which is a kind of metal used to make, as the name suggests, tools that can withstand high temperatures. As lasers liquified the metal and different crystals emerged, X-ray beams probed the samples with enough energy and speed to produce images of the fleeting process. The team members required two separate facilities to support the cooling rates they wanted to test, which ranged from temperatures of tens of thousands to more than a million kelvins per second.

Furthermore, this development could potentially enhance search and rescue missions, such as locating a missing individual in a large area, as well as military and police surveillance operations. 
Notably, the ability to image scenes outside an observer's direct line of sight can often greatly improve the effectiveness of these operations. 
It is worth noting that this capability may also tend to improve robotic vision and the safety of self-driving vehicles in the future. 
Ultimately, the potential applications of this technology appear to be numerous. 
In essence, the method involves reconstructing a full image of a hidden object or obstacle, which can often be a complex process. 
Additionally, most conventional methods of imaging objects behind an obstruction typically utilize an external source of light, such as ultra-short pulses of visible or infrared laser light. 
This highlights the challenges associated with imaging hidden objects using only visible and infrared light, which can often be limited by the rough surface of a typical wall. 
Furthermore, the rough surface of a wall tends to scatter incoming light in all directions, revealing less information about concealed objects. 
It is worth noting that this limitation may require sophisticated algorithms and significant computing time to create even a semi-sharp image. 
Notably, the use of visible and infrared light may also tip off adversaries that they are under surveillance, which can often be a significant drawback. 
Ultimately, the development of new methods for imaging concealed objects may lead to improved outcomes in a variety of applications, and this technology appears to be an important area of research. 
In summary, the new method of imaging concealed objects has the potential to enhance search and rescue missions, military and police surveillance operations, and robotic vision, and may tend to lead to significant improvements in these areas.
output:
A new way of imaging concealed objects, devised by a researcher at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and his colleagues, might take all the fun out of hide-and-seek, but could also help save lives.

Imaging scenes that lie outside an observer’s direct line of sight could greatly enhance search and rescue missions, such as finding a lost child in an abandoned factory, as well as military and police surveillance operations, such as exposing a hidden terrorist or enemy stronghold. The ability to see around corners and reconstruct a full image of a hidden object or obstacle in real time also could someday improve robotic vision and the safety and accuracy of self-driving cars. (At present, the prototype method cannot create an image instantaneously.)

Most conventional methods used to image objects behind an obstruction use an external source of light — ultra-short pulses of visible or infrared laser light, for example. The light source initially illuminates a wall that scatters the light into the concealed region. When the light strikes a hidden object, the object re-scatters some of the light back to the wall where it can be detected.

However, imaging hidden objects using only visible and infrared light is challenging. At those relatively short wavelengths, a typical wall — no matter how smooth to the human touch — presents itself as a rough surface and scatters incoming light in all directions. It therefore reveals less information about objects than light reflected from a smooth or mirrored surface and requires sophisticated algorithms and significant computing time to create even a semi-sharp image. In addition, the illumination could tip off adversaries that they are under surveillance.

In Gaithersburg, Maryland, it is worth noting that the U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has entered into a cooperative research and development agreement, commonly referred to as a CRADA, with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. This partnership aims to initiate the development of standards and testing protocols for an innovative generation of breathalyzers that may have the capability to diagnose malaria and tuberculosis (TB). 

Furthermore, under the auspices of this CRADA, NIST researchers are expected to embark on a new initiative to create tools and techniques that can often ensure the accuracy and reliability of these breathalyzers. This quality will likely be essential should these devices reach the market and be implemented in developing regions across the globe. 

Notably, several manufacturers and academic institutions are involved in the development of breathalyzers targeting malaria and TB, which are recognized as some of the leading contributors to mortality on a global scale. According to Kavita Jeerage, a materials research engineer at NIST, breath-based diagnostics may soon find applications in identifying or monitoring the progression of various conditions and diseases, which can include liver disease, multiple sclerosis, and cancer. 

In her remarks, Jeerage expressed enthusiasm about participating in this significant global initiative. She stated that through this collaboration, they aim to establish the foundation necessary to ensure the highest levels of accuracy and effectiveness for the forthcoming generation of breathalyzers. 

It is important to acknowledge that malaria and TB are responsible for approximately 2 million fatalities annually. Typically, healthcare professionals diagnose malaria through the use of blood tests, while TB is identified through the collection of sputum samples. 

Both procedures, however, tend to be costly and generally require access to sophisticated technical equipment and often a laboratory for sample analysis. Additionally, certain strains of the malaria parasite may have developed the ability to evade detection. In summary, the collaboration between NIST and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation may contribute significantly to improving diagnostic tools for these critical infectious diseases.
output:

Under the CRADA, NIST researchers will launch a new effort to develop tools and techniques for ensuring that the breathalyzers are accurate and reliable, which will be vital should they come to market and be deployed throughout the developing world.

But according to NIST materials research engineer Kavita Jeerage, breath-based diagnostics may soon be used to identify or monitor the progression of a wide range of conditions and diseases, including liver disease, multiple sclerosis and cancer.

“We are thrilled to be participating in this global effort to develop new breath tests for infectious disease,” Jeerage said. “Through this partnership, we will lay the groundwork to ensure the highest levels of accuracy and efficacy for the next generation of breathalyzers.”

So they went up to the Mock Turtle, who looked at them with large eyes full of tears, but said nothing.

So they sat down, and nobody spoke for some minutes. Alice thought to herself, “I don’t see how he can ever finish, if he doesn’t begin.” But she waited patiently.

An enormous puppy gazed down at her with large, round eyes, and feebly extended one paw, attempting to make contact with her. "Poor little creature!" remarked Alice in a coaxing tone, as she earnestly attempted to whistle to it; however, she was persistently terrified at the thought that it might be hungry, which could result in its consuming her despite her efforts at coaxing.

Barely aware of her actions, she picked up a small stick and offered it to the puppy. Consequently, the puppy leaped into the air, propelling itself off all four feet simultaneously with a delighted yelp, and rushed towards the stick, feigning an intent to worry it. In response, Alice sought refuge behind a large thistle to avoid being overwhelmed. The moment she reappeared on the opposite side, the puppy made another dash for the stick, tumbling head over heels in its eagerness to seize it. Alice, perceiving the situation as reminiscent of engaging in play with a cart-horse and anticipating the imminent possibility of being trampled, circled back around the thistle. Subsequently, the puppy initiated a series of brief charges toward the stick, moving only a short distance forward each time while retreating a considerable distance back, all the while barking hoarsely. Eventually, it settled down at a distance, panting, with its tongue lolling out of its mouth and its large eyes partially closed.
output:
An enormous puppy was looking down at her with large round eyes, and feebly stretching out one paw, trying to touch her. “Poor little thing!” said Alice, in a coaxing tone, and she tried hard to whistle to it; but she was terribly frightened all the time at the thought that it might be hungry, in which case it would be very likely to eat her up in spite of all her coaxing.

Hardly knowing what she did, she picked up a little bit of stick, and held it out to the puppy; whereupon the puppy jumped into the air off all its feet at once, with a yelp of delight, and rushed at the stick, and made believe to worry it; then Alice dodged behind a great thistle, to keep herself from being run over; and the moment she appeared on the other side, the puppy made another rush at the stick, and tumbled head over heels in its hurry to get hold of it; then Alice, thinking it was very like having a game of play with a cart-horse, and expecting every moment to be trampled under its feet, ran round the thistle again; then the puppy began a series of short charges at the stick, running a very little way forwards each time and a long way back, and barking hoarsely all the while, till at last it sat down a good way off, panting, with its tongue hanging out of its mouth, and its great eyes half shut.

output: The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo: she succeeded in getting its body tucked away, comfortably enough, under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but generally, just as she had got its neck nicely straightened out, and was going to give the hedgehog a blow with its head, it would twist itself round and look up in her face, with such a puzzled expression that she could not help bursting out laughing: and when she had got its head down, and was going to begin again, it was very provoking to find that the hedgehog had unrolled itself, and was in the act of crawling away: besides all this, there was generally a ridge or furrow in the way wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog to, and, as the doubled-up soldiers were always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, Alice soon came to the conclusion that it was a very difficult game indeed.

While she sometimes found her presence tiresome, the contrast to her current situation was stark. Now, she was alone and beginning to learn how to dress herself, as Martha often looked at her with a sense of disapproval when she requested assistance.
output: Mary’s meals were served regularly, and Martha waited on her, but no one troubled themselves about her in the least. Mrs. Medlock came and looked at her every day or two, but no one inquired what she did or told her what to do. She supposed that perhaps this was the English way of treating children. In India she had always been attended by her Ayah, who had followed her about and waited on her, hand and foot. She had often been tired of her company. Now she was followed by nobody and was learning to dress herself because Martha looked as though she thought she was silly and stupid when she wanted to have things handed to her and put on.

He struggled throughout the day, breathing heavily like an old buccaneer suffering from an apoplectic fit. Unfortunately, his chest had been crushed by the impact, and his skull was fractured from the fall. Sometime during the following night, without any sign or sound, he passed away.
output: Out of the eight men who had fallen in the action, only three still breathed - that one of the pirates who had been shot at the loophole, Hunter, and Captain Smollett; and of these, the first two were as good as dead; the mutineer indeed died under the doctor’s knife, and Hunter, do what we could, never recovered consciousness in this world. He lingered all day, breathing loudly like the old buccaneer at home in his apoplectic fit, but the bones of his chest had been crushed by the blow and his skull fractured in falling, and some time in the following night, without sign or sound, he went to his Maker.

output: Perhaps it was this - perhaps it was the look of the island, with its grey, melancholy woods, and wild stone spires, and the surf that we could both see and hear foaming and thundering on the steep beach - at least, although the sun shone bright and hot, and the shore birds were fishing and crying all around us, and you would have thought anyone would have been glad to get to land after being so long at sea, my heart sank, as the saying is, into my boots; and from the first look onward, I hated the very thought of Treasure Island.

input: The eyes of moles and certain burrowing rodents are rudimentary in size, and in some cases they are entirely covered by skin and fur. This condition of the eyes is probably the result of gradual reduction through disuse, although it may also have been aided by natural selection. In South America, a burrowing rodent known as the tuco-tuco, or Ctenomys, is even more subterranean in its habits than the mole. A Spaniard who had often caught these animals assured me that they were frequently blind. One that I kept alive was certainly in this condition, and dissection showed that the cause was inflammation of the nictitating membrane. Since frequent inflammation of the eyes must be harmful to any animal, and since eyes are certainly not indispensable to animals with subterranean habits, a reduction in their size, together with the adhesion of the eyelids and the growth of fur over them, might in such a case be an advantage. If this were so, natural selection would constantly aid the effects of disuse.

input: In the case of animals with separate sexes, the capacity to prevent crosses constitutes an important element of success in the formation of new races, at least in a country that is already stocked with other races. Additionally, in this respect the enclosure of the land plays a part. Moreover, wandering savages or the inhabitants of open plains rarely possess more than one breed of the same species. Furthermore, pigeons can be mated for life, and this is a great convenience to the fancier, for in this manner many races may be kept true, though mingled in the same aviary, and this circumstance must have largely favoured the improvement and formation of new breeds. It is worth noting that pigeons, I may add, can be propagated in great numbers and at a very quick rate, and inferior birds may be freely rejected, since when killed they serve for food. In essence, on the other hand, cats, from their nocturnal rambling habits, cannot be matched, and, although so much valued by women and children, we hardly ever see a distinct breed kept up; such breeds as we do sometimes see are almost always imported from some other country, often from islands. Additionally, although I do not doubt that some domestic animals vary less than others, yet the rarity or absence of distinct breeds of the cat, the donkey, peacock, goose, and so forth, may be attributed in main part to selection not having been brought into play: in cats, from the difficulty in pairing them; in donkeys, from only a few being kept by poor people, and little attention paid to their breeding; in peacocks, from not being very easily reared and a large stock not kept; in geese, from being valuable only for two purposes, food and feathers, and more especially from no pleasure having been felt in the display of distinct breeds.

input: This highlights the observation that we know nothing about the origin or history of any of our domestic breeds. In reality, a breed, much like a dialect of a language, can hardly be said to have had a definite origin. A man preserves and breeds from an individual with some slight deviation of structure, or takes more care than usual in matching his best animals, thereby improving them, and the improved individuals slowly spread in the immediate neighbourhood. At this stage, however, they will hardly have a distinct name, and since they are only slightly valued, their history will be disregarded. When further improved through the same slow and gradual process, they will spread more widely and come to be recognised as something distinct and valuable, and will then probably first receive a provincial name. In semi-civilised countries with little free communication, the spreading and knowledge of any new sub-breed will be a slow process. Once the points of value of the new sub-breed are fully acknowledged, the principle of unconscious selection will always tend to slowly add to the characteristic features of the breed, whatever they may be, perhaps more at one period than another as the breed rises or falls in fashion, and perhaps more in one district than another according to the state of civilisation of the inhabitants. Ultimately, the chance of any record having been preserved of such slow, varying, and insensible changes will be infinitely small.
output: I think these views further explain what has sometimes been noticed - namely that we know nothing about the origin or history of any of our domestic breeds. But, in fact, a breed, like a dialect of a language, can hardly be said to have had a definite origin. A man preserves and breeds from an individual with some slight deviation of structure, or takes more care than usual in matching his best animals and thus improves them, and the improved individuals slowly spread in the immediate neighbourhood. But as yet they will hardly have a distinct name, and from being only slightly valued, their history will be disregarded. When further improved by the same slow and gradual process, they will spread more widely, and will get recognised as something distinct and valuable, and will then probably first receive a provincial name. As soon as the points of value of the new sub-breed are once fully acknowledged, the principle, as I have called it, of unconscious selection will always tend, - perhaps more at one period than at another, as the breed rises or falls in fashion, - perhaps more in one district than in another, according to the state of civilisation of the inhabitants - slowly to add to the characteristic features of the breed, whatever they may be. But the chance will be infinitely small of any record having been preserved of such slow, varying, and insensible changes.

input: It is important to note that the process may not occur as consistently as illustrated in the diagram, even if it is somewhat irregular. It is not necessarily the case that the most distinct varieties will always dominate and reproduce; a more moderate form may often persist for extended periods and might or might not lead to more than one altered descendant. Natural selection typically operates based on the specific characteristics of environments that are either unoccupied or not fully occupied by other organisms, which can be influenced by a multitude of complex interactions. Generally speaking, the more varied in structure the descendants from a single species can become, the better their chances of exploiting different niches, which may lead to an increase in their modified offspring. In the diagram, the line of succession appears to be interrupted at regular intervals, indicated by small numbered letters that represent the distinct forms recognized as varieties. However, these interruptions are theoretical and could have been placed at various points, assuming sufficient time for significant divergent variation to accumulate. Overall, the complexity of these processes highlights the nuanced nature of evolutionary change.
output: But I must here remark that I do not suppose that the process ever goes on so regularly as is represented in the diagram, though in itself made somewhat irregular. I am far from thinking that the most divergent varieties will invariably prevail and multiply: a medium form may often long endure, and may or may not produce more than one modified descendant; for natural selection will always act according to the nature of the places which are either unoccupied or not perfectly occupied by other beings; and this will depend on infinitely complex relations. But as a general rule, the more diversified in structure the descendants from any one species can be rendered, the more places they will be enabled to seize on, and the more their modified progeny will be increased. In our diagram the line of succession is broken at regular intervals by small numbered letters marking the successive forms which have become sufficiently distinct to be recorded as varieties. But these breaks are imaginary, and might have been inserted anywhere, after intervals long enough to have allowed the accumulation of a considerable amount of divergent variation.

input: This passage summarizes the conditions that can influence natural selection, focusing on both favorable and unfavorable factors. It suggests that a large continental area, which is likely to experience significant fluctuations in elevation, is conducive to the emergence of diverse life forms that may thrive and expand over time. Initially, when this area exists as a continent, its diverse population will face intense competition. As subsidence transforms the continent into separate islands, many individuals of the same species will remain on each island, leading to restricted interbreeding at the edges of their ranges. This isolation, coupled with any physical changes, will hinder immigration, necessitating that new ecological niches be filled by adaptations of existing species. Over time, these modifications can lead to well-defined varieties. Should the islands eventually be uplifted back into a continental form, competition will resurge, allowing the more advantageous varieties to proliferate. This process may result in the extinction of less adapted forms, altering the relative proportions of the continent's inhabitants and providing further opportunities for natural selection to drive the evolution of new species.
output: To sum up the circumstances favourable and unfavourable to natural selection, as far as the extreme intricacy of the subject permits. I conclude, looking to the future, that for terrestrial productions a large continental area, which will probably undergo many oscillations of level, and which consequently will exist for long periods in a broken condition, will be the most favourable for the production of many new forms of life, likely to endure long and to spread widely. For the area will first have existed as a continent, and the inhabitants, at this period numerous in individuals and kinds, will have been subjected to very severe competition. When converted by subsidence into large separate islands, there will still exist many individuals of the same species on each island: intercrossing on the confines of the range of each species will thus be checked: after physical changes of any kind, immigration will be prevented, so that new places in the polity of each island will have to be filled up by modifications of the old inhabitants; and time will be allowed for the varieties in each to become well modified and perfected. When, by renewed elevation, the islands shall be re-converted into a continental area, there will again be severe competition: the most favoured or improved varieties will be enabled to spread: there will be much extinction of the less improved forms, and the relative proportional numbers of the various inhabitants of the renewed continent will again be changed; and again there will be a fair field for natural selection to improve still further the inhabitants, and thus produce new species.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: Natural selection may be a powerful process when compared to human selection, influencing traits that might seem trivial in importance. It appears to operate across various ages and can affect both males and females. Sexual selection also plays a role in this process. There tends to be a general tendency for interbreeding among individuals of the same species, which can be influenced by both favorable and unfavorable conditions for natural selection, including factors such as intercrossing, isolation, and population size. The effects of natural selection may often be slow and gradual, and it can lead to extinction in certain cases. The divergence of characteristics seems to be linked to the variety of organisms in small areas and the process of naturalization. Overall, the actions of natural selection through the divergence of traits and extinction contribute to the evolution of descendants from a shared ancestor, providing an explanation for the categorization of all living organisms.
output: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species. Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction caused by Natural Selection. Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation. Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings.

input: If species are considered to be distinct and stable varieties, it may be easier to understand why their hybrid offspring might exhibit similar complex patterns in terms of resemblance to their parents. This includes being blended through successive crossings and other related characteristics, much like the hybrid offspring of recognized varieties. Conversely, these observations could appear puzzling if species were created independently while varieties were formed through secondary processes. Ultimately, this raises important questions about the nature of species and varieties in the context of their relationships and origins.
output: If species be only well-marked and permanent varieties, we can at once see why their crossed offspring should follow the same complex laws in their degrees and kinds of resemblance to their parents, - in being absorbed into each other by successive crosses, and in other such points, - as do the crossed offspring of acknowledged varieties. On the other hand, these would be strange facts if species have been independently created, and varieties have been produced by secondary laws.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

I recalled everything quite clearly; the language, the look, and the tone felt momentarily refreshed. I found myself in the classroom where Adèle was drawing. I leaned over her to guide her pencil, and she glanced up, surprised. 

“What is it, Miss?” she asked. “Your fingers are trembling like a leaf, and your cheeks are red — so red, like cherries!” 

I quickly tried to push away the unpleasant thought I had been forming about Grace Poole; it was unsettling to me. When I compared myself to her, I noticed our differences. Bessie Leaven had mentioned that I was quite a lady, and there was truth to that—I recognized that I was indeed a lady. In that moment, I felt I appeared much better than I did when Bessie last saw me; I had more color, more fullness, and a greater sense of vitality and enthusiasm, likely due to my brighter hopes and more profound joys.
output:
I well remembered all; language, glance, and tone seemed at the moment vividly renewed. I was now in the schoolroom; Adèle was drawing; I bent over her and directed her pencil. She looked up with a sort of start.

“Qu’avez-vous, mademoiselle?” said she. “Vos doigts tremblent comme la feuille, et vos joues sont rouges: mais, rouges comme des cerises!”

I hastened to drive from my mind the hateful notion I had been conceiving respecting Grace Poole; it disgusted me. I compared myself with her, and found we were different. Bessie Leaven had said I was quite a lady; and she spoke truth - I was a lady. And now I looked much better than I did when Bessie saw me; I had more colour and more flesh, more life, more vivacity, because I had brighter hopes and keener enjoyments.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: The speaker expresses a clear position on their feelings toward Mr. Wickham, stating that they are not in love with him at present. output: “I beg your pardon. I will try again. At present I am not in love with Mr. Wickham; no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison, the most agreeable man I ever saw - and if he becomes really attached to me - I believe it will be better that he should not. I see the imprudence of it. Oh, that abominable Mr. Darcy! My father’s opinion of me does me the greatest honour; and I should be miserable to forfeit it. My father, however, is partial to Mr. Wickham. In short, my dear aunt, I should be very sorry to be the means of making any of you unhappy; but since we see, every day, that where there is affection young people are seldom withheld, by immediate want of fortune, from entering into engagements with each other, how can I promise to be wiser than so many of my fellow-creatures, if I am tempted, or how am I even to know that it would be wiser to resist? All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry. I will not be in a hurry to believe myself his first object. When I am in company with him, I will not be wishing. In short, I will do my best.”

As Mr. Darcy approached, seemingly without any intention of engaging in conversation, Miss Lucas challenged her friend to bring up a particular topic. This prompted Elizabeth to address him directly, asking, “Did you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself particularly well just now when I was encouraging Colonel Forster to organize a ball at Meryton?” 

Mr. Darcy responded, noting, “You are quite an unusual friend, always wanting me to perform for everyone. If I were more vain about my musical abilities, you would be quite helpful; however, I would prefer not to perform in front of those who are accustomed to hearing the best.” Despite his reluctance, he acquiesced when Miss Lucas persisted, saying, “Very well; if it must be done, then it shall be.” He then looked at Mr. Darcy and referenced an old saying that everyone present would know, stating, “Keep your breath to cool your porridge,” and concluded that he would reserve his breath for singing.
output:
On his approaching them soon afterwards, though without seeming to have any intention of speaking, Miss Lucas defied her friend to mention such a subject to him, which immediately provoking Elizabeth to do it, she turned to him and said, -

“Did not you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself uncommonly well just now, when I was teasing Colonel Forster to give us a ball at Meryton?”

“You are a very strange creature by way of a friend! - always wanting me to play and sing before anybody and everybody! If my vanity had taken a musical turn, you would have been invaluable; but as it is, I would really rather not sit down before those who must be in the habit of hearing the very best performers.” On Miss Lucas’s persevering, however, she added, “Very well; if it must be so, it must.” And gravely glancing at Mr. Darcy, “There is a very fine old saying, which everybody here is of course familiar with - ‘Keep your breath to cool your porridge,’ - and I shall keep mine to swell my song.”
title: Pride and Prejudice

Placing them next to your great-uncle the judge could be fitting, as they share a similar profession, albeit in different areas. Regarding your Elizabeth’s portrait, it may be best to reconsider having it painted, as it can be quite challenging for any artist to accurately capture those lovely eyes. 

While it may be difficult to fully convey their expression, an artist might still be able to replicate their color, shape, and the notably fine eyelashes.
output:
“Oh yes. Do let the portraits of your uncle and aunt Philips be placed in the gallery at Pemberley. Put them next to your great-uncle the judge. They are in the same profession, you know, only in different lines. As for your Elizabeth’s picture, you must not attempt to have it taken, for what painter could do justice to those beautiful eyes?”

“It would not be easy, indeed, to catch their expression; but their colour and shape, and the eyelashes, so remarkably fine, might be copied.”
title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen

input:
Miss Havisham sat in silence, her head resting in her hands, making a low sound of distress while gently rocking in her chair, but she did not respond. 

"Or," Estella suggested, "if you had taught her, from the very beginning of her understanding, with all your strength and effort, that daylight existed, but that it was her adversary and could harm her, leading her to turn away from it because it had caused you pain and would likely do the same to her; if you had instilled this belief, and later wished for her to embrace the daylight naturally but she found it difficult to do so, you might have felt disappointed and upset, wouldn’t you?" 

In summary, the conversation reflects the complexities of expectations and the potential impact of early beliefs on an individual's relationship with the world.
output:
Miss Havisham, with her head in her hands, sat making a low moaning, and swaying herself on her chair, but gave no answer.

“Or,” said Estella, - “which is a nearer case, - if you had taught her, from the dawn of her intelligence, with your utmost energy and might, that there was such a thing as daylight, but that it was made to be her enemy and destroyer, and she must always turn against it, for it had blighted you and would else blight her; - if you had done this, and then, for a purpose, had wanted her to take naturally to the daylight and she could not do it, you would have been disappointed and angry?”
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: The observations discussed indicate that the composition of legislative bodies is primarily influenced by the interests and perspectives of various community classes. Regardless of whether representation is extensive or limited, it tends to consist predominantly of landowners, merchants, and professionals who effectively represent these diverse interests. While it may be noted that other types of individuals have been observed in local legislatures, these cases are exceptions and not numerous enough to significantly change the overall characteristics of the government. Strong individuals from all backgrounds can overcome challenges posed by their circumstances and gain recognition for their abilities, receiving respect from both their specific groups and society at large. Ideally, opportunities should be accessible to everyone. It is hoped that examples of notable individuals will emerge in both federal and state legislation. However, such instances do not undermine the reasoning based on the prevailing patterns observed.
output: WE HAVE seen that the result of the observations, to which the foregoing number has been principally devoted, is, that from the natural operation of the different interests and views of the various classes of the community, whether the representation of the people be more or less numerous, it will consist almost entirely of proprietors of land, of merchants, and of members of the learned professions, who will truly represent all those different interests and views. If it should be objected that we have seen other descriptions of men in the local legislatures, I answer that it is admitted there are exceptions to the rule, but not in sufficient number to influence the general complexion or character of the government. There are strong minds in every walk of life that will rise superior to the disadvantages of situation, and will command the tribute due to their merit, not only from the classes to which they particularly belong, but from the society in general. The door ought to be equally open to all; and I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we shall see examples of such vigorous plants flourishing in the soil of federal as well as of State legislation; but occasional instances of this sort will not render the reasoning founded upon the general course of things, less conclusive.
title: The Federalist Papers
author: Alexander Hamilton

input:
The importance of having a Constitution that is at least as effective as the one being proposed for maintaining the Union is the issue we are currently examining. 

This discussion may be divided into three main areas: the goals that the federal government should address, the amount of authority needed to achieve those goals, and the individuals who should be subject to that authority. The organization and distribution of this power will be more appropriately considered in the following section.
output:
THE necessity of a Constitution, at least equally energetic with the one proposed, to the preservation of the Union, is the point at the examination of which we are now arrived.

This inquiry will naturally divide itself into three branches - the objects to be provided for by the federal government, the quantity of power necessary to the accomplishment of those objects, the persons upon whom that power ought to operate. Its distribution and organization will more properly claim our attention under the succeeding head.
title: The Federalist Papers
author: Alexander Hamilton

output:
If, under this impression, he proceeded to pass in review the several State constitutions, how great would be his disappointment to find that TWO ONLY of them(1) contained an interdiction of standing armies in time of peace; that the other eleven had either observed a profound silence on the subject, or had in express terms admitted the right of the Legislature to authorize their existence.

Still, however he would be persuaded that there must be some plausible foundation for the cry raised on this head. title: The Federalist Papers
author: Alexander Hamilton

input: Another resource for influencing how European nations act toward us in this area may come from establishing a federal navy. It seems likely that if the Union continues under an effective government, we would be in a position, before too long, to build a navy that, while it might not match those of the major maritime powers, could still carry respectable weight if added to the scale of either of two contending sides. This tends to be especially true with regard to operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent at the right time to reinforce either side, could often be enough to determine the outcome of a campaign, and matters of the greatest importance might depend on that outcome. Our position in this respect is a very strong one. If we also consider how useful supplies from this country can be in carrying out military operations in the West Indies, it can readily be seen that such a favorable situation would allow us to negotiate with considerable advantage for commercial privileges. A price could be placed not only on our friendship but also on our neutrality. By steadily adhering to the Union, we may hope before long to become the arbiter of Europe in America and to be able to tilt the balance of European rivalries in this part of the world as our interests may require.
output: A further resource for influencing the conduct of European nations toward us, in this respect, would arise from the establishment of a federal navy. There can be no doubt that the continuance of the Union under an efficient government would put it in our power, at a period not very distant, to create a navy which, if it could not vie with those of the great maritime powers, would at least be of respectable weight if thrown into the scale of either of two contending parties. This would be more peculiarly the case in relation to operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent opportunely to the reinforcement of either side, would often be sufficient to decide the fate of a campaign, on the event of which interests of the greatest magnitude were suspended. Our position is, in this respect, a most commanding one. And if to this consideration we add that of the usefulness of supplies from this country, in the prosecution of military operations in the West Indies, it will readily be perceived that a situation so favorable would enable us to bargain with great advantage for commercial privileges. A price would be set not only upon our friendship, but upon our neutrality. By a steady adherence to the Union we may hope, erelong, to become the arbiter of Europe in America, and to be able to incline the balance of European competitions in this part of the world as our interest may dictate.
title: The Federalist Papers
author: Alexander Hamilton

input: Upon returning home, Lydgate received a visit from Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar had not been in town the previous day, but news of an execution at Lydgate's residence reached Lowick by evening, carried by Mr. Spicer, the shoemaker and parish clerk, who learned it from his brother, a respected bell-hanger in Lowick Gate. Since the evening when Lydgate descended from the billiard room with Fred Vincy, Mr. Farebrother's thoughts about him had turned rather somber. While playing at the Green Dragon might seem trivial for another man, in Lydgate, it appeared to be one of several indicators that he was becoming different from his former self. He was starting to engage in activities that he had previously regarded with disdain. Although some whispers about dissatisfaction in Lydgate's marriage might have contributed to this change, Mr. Farebrother suspected that the primary issue was the growing reports of Lydgate's debts, leading him to worry that any belief in Lydgate's hidden resources or support could be misguided. The disappointment he had faced in his initial attempt to earn Lydgate's trust made him hesitant to try again, but the news of the execution taking place in the house prompted the Vicar to set aside his reluctance.
output: On returning home Lydgate had a visit from Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar had not been in the town the day before, but the news that there was an execution in Lydgate’s house had got to Lowick by the evening, having been carried by Mr. Spicer, shoemaker and parish-clerk, who had it from his brother, the respectable bell-hanger in Lowick Gate. Since that evening when Lydgate had come down from the billiard room with Fred Vincy, Mr. Farebrother’s thoughts about him had been rather gloomy. Playing at the Green Dragon once or oftener might have been a trifle in another man; but in Lydgate it was one of several signs that he was getting unlike his former self. He was beginning to do things for which he had formerly even an excessive scorn. Whatever certain dissatisfactions in marriage, which some silly tinklings of gossip had given him hints of, might have to do with this change, Mr. Farebrother felt sure that it was chiefly connected with the debts which were being more and more distinctly reported, and he began to fear that any notion of Lydgate’s having resources or friends in the background must be quite illusory. The rebuff he had met with in his first attempt to win Lydgate’s confidence, disinclined him to a second; but this news of the execution being actually in the house, determined the Vicar to overcome his reluctance.
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input: “I shall be exceedingly grateful if you would be willing to visit me here from time to time, Mr. Lydgate,” the banker remarked following a moment of contemplation. “If, as I cautiously anticipate, I am fortunate enough to have you as a valuable collaborator in the intriguing subject of hospital administration, there will be numerous matters that we must address in a confidential setting. Regarding the new hospital, which is nearly complete, I will reflect on your comments concerning the benefits of a specialized facility for treating fevers. The ultimate decision will be mine, as although Lord Medlicote has generously provided the land and timber for the construction, he is not inclined to dedicate his personal attention to this endeavor.”
output: “I shall be exceedingly obliged if you will look in on me here occasionally, Mr. Lydgate,” the banker observed, after a brief pause. “If, as I dare to hope, I have the privilege of finding you a valuable coadjutor in the interesting matter of hospital management, there will be many questions which we shall need to discuss in private. As to the new hospital, which is nearly finished, I shall consider what you have said about the advantages of the special destination for fevers. The decision will rest with me, for though Lord Medlicote has given the land and timber for the building, he is not disposed to give his personal attention to the object.”
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input: Some may argue that once relations with Britain are repaired, the country will provide protection. This raises the question of whether it is wise to suggest that Britain would maintain a navy in our ports for that purpose. Common sense indicates that a power that has sought to conquer us is not the most appropriate choice for our defense. This highlights the potential for conquest to occur under the guise of friendship, risking that, after a prolonged and courageous struggle, we could be deceived into a state of subjugation. If British ships are not allowed in our harbors, one might wonder how they could effectively safeguard us. A navy located three or four thousand miles away would have limited utility, particularly during urgent situations. Ultimately, if we must defend ourselves, it stands to reason that we should do so independently rather than relying on another nation.
output: Some, perhaps, will say, that after we have made it up with Britain, she will protect us. Can we be so unwise as to mean, that she shall keep a navy in our harbours for that purpose? Common sense will tell us, that the power which hath endeavoured to subdue us, is of all others, the most improper to defend us. Conquest may be effected under the pretence of friendship; and ourselves, after a long and brave resistance, be at last cheated into slavery. And if her ships are not to be admitted into our harbours, I would ask, how is she to protect us? A navy three or four thousand miles off can be of little use, and on sudden emergencies, none at all. Wherefore, if we must hereafter protect ourselves, why not do it for ourselves? Why do it for another?
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The contest for the monarchy and succession, between the Houses of York and Lancaster, subjected England to a prolonged period of violence. Over the course of this conflict, twelve major battles, in addition to various skirmishes and sieges, were waged between Henry and Edward. On two occasions, Henry was taken captive by Edward, only to find himself in a similar position at the hands of Henry. Furthermore, the unpredictable nature of warfare and the sentiments of a nation are evident, particularly when personal disputes serve as the foundation for conflict. This is illustrated by the fact that Henry was triumphantly escorted from a prison to a palace, while Edward was compelled to flee from a palace to a foreign land. However, as is often the case with abrupt changes in fortune, such transitions are rarely enduring; thus, Henry was ultimately displaced from the throne, and Edward was reinstated to succeed him. It is worth noting that Parliament consistently aligned itself with the faction that appeared strongest.
output: The contest for monarchy and succession, between the houses of York and Lancaster, laid England in a scene of blood for many years. Twelve pitched battles, besides skirmishes and sieges, were fought between Henry and Edward. Twice was Henry prisoner to Edward, who in his turn was prisoner to Henry. And so uncertain is the fate of war and the temper of a nation, when nothing but personal matters are the ground of a quarrel, that Henry was taken in triumph from a prison to a palace, and Edward obliged to fly from a palace to a foreign land; yet, as sudden transitions of temper are seldom lasting, Henry in his turn was driven from the throne, and Edward recalled to succeed him. The parliament always following the strongest side.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Immediate necessity can render certain actions convenient, but if such actions continue unchecked, they may lead to oppression. It is important to distinguish between expedience and what is right. During the crises that America faced, the appointment of representatives from various Houses of Assembly was a practical and appropriate solution for consultation, and this approach helped to protect the continent from disaster. However, it is likely that a Congress will always be in existence, and it is essential for those invested in maintaining order to consider how its members are chosen. This raises a question for those who study human behavior: is it wise for a single group of individuals to hold both representation and election powers? As we plan for future generations, it is crucial to recognize that virtue is not something that can be inherited.
output: Immediate necessity makes many things convenient, which if continued would grow into oppressions. Expedience and right are different things. When the calamities of America required a consultation, there was no method so ready, or at that time so proper, as to appoint persons from the several Houses of Assembly for that purpose; and the wisdom with which they have proceeded hath preserved this continent from ruin. But as it is more than probable that we shall never be without a Congress, every well wisher to good order, must own, that the mode for choosing members of that body, deserves consideration. And I put it as a question to those, who make a study of mankind, whether representation and election is not too great a power for one and the same body of men to possess? When we are planning for posterity, we ought to remember, that virtue is not hereditary.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
It may be suggested that describing the constitution of England as a union of three powers that check each other may overlook some complexities, as this characterization might not fully capture the nuances involved. 

Firstly, it can often be argued that the monarchy may present a tendency towards seeking absolute power, which implies the necessity of oversight to ensure that such ambitions are kept in check. 

Secondly, there is a notion that the Commons, due to their appointment, may be viewed as more prudent or deserving of trust compared to the crown. 

In summary, the relationship among the powers within the English constitution is complex and may be subject to differing interpretations.
output:
To say that the constitution of England is a union of three powers reciprocally checking each other, is farcical, either the words have no meaning, or they are flat contradictions.

First. - That the king is not to be trusted without being looked after, or in other words, that a thirst for absolute power is the natural disease of monarchy.

Secondly. - That the commons, by being appointed for that purpose, are either wiser or more worthy of confidence than the crown.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Human beings may have started as equals in the process of creation, and this equality could only have been altered by later circumstances. The differences between wealth and poverty can often be explained, perhaps without needing to resort to the more severe terms of oppression and greed. While oppression can frequently be a result of wealth disparities, it is rarely the direct cause of them. Additionally, while greed may help someone avoid severe financial hardship, it often makes them too cautious to achieve true wealth. In summary, the dynamics of equality and wealth are complex and influenced by various factors.
output: Mankind being originally equals in the order of creation, the equality could only be destroyed by some subsequent circumstance; the distinctions of rich, and poor, may in a great measure be accounted for, and that without having recourse to the harsh ill sounding names of oppression and avarice. Oppression is often the consequence, but seldom or never the means of riches; and though avarice will preserve a man from being necessitously poor, it generally makes him too timorous to be wealthy.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine
