Emma found herself somewhat entertained by the idea that it was quite unusual and felt she had no defense for him. 

“I really cannot understand,” Mrs. Elton remarked, feeling the slight as any wife might, “how he could possibly do such a thing to you, of all people! You are certainly the last person one would think could be overlooked! My dear Mr. E., I am confident he must have left a message for you. Not even Knightley could be that forgetful; it must be that his servants overlooked it. I think that is likely the situation, especially with the Donwell staff, who, as I have frequently noted, can be rather clumsy and forgetful. I certainly would not allow someone like his Harry to serve at our sideboard for any reason. And regarding Mrs. Hodges, Wright does not hold her in high regard at all. She promised him a receipt but failed to send it.” 

In summary, Mrs. Elton conveys her disbelief at the situation and expresses her confidence that a misunderstanding has occurred due to the negligence of others.
output:
Emma amused herself by protesting that it was very extraordinary, indeed, and that she had not a syllable to say for him.

“I cannot imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, (feeling the indignity as a wife ought to do,) “I cannot imagine how he could do such a thing by you, of all people in the world! The very last person whom one should expect to be forgotten! - My dear Mr. E., he must have left a message for you, I am sure he must. - Not even Knightley could be so very eccentric; - and his servants forgot it. Depend upon it, that was the case: and very likely to happen with the Donwell servants, who are all, I have often observed, extremely awkward and remiss. - I am sure I would not have such a creature as his Harry stand at our sideboard for any consideration. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright holds her very cheap indeed. - She promised Wright a receipt, and never sent it.”
title: Emma
author: Jane Austen

input: Mrs. Weston responded to the conclusion, as she had a high regard for Frank in most aspects and a strong affection for him. This highlights the earnestness of her defense, which was characterized by a balance of rational argument and emotional investment. She presented her points with a great deal of reason and affection, but ultimately, Emma's attention was diverted, shifting to either Brunswick Square or Donwell. As a result, Emma failed to fully engage with Mrs. Weston's comments and had to pause before responding to her final statement, "We have not yet had the letter we are so anxious for, you know, but I hope it will soon come." This suggests that Emma had not been closely following the conversation, as she was forced to answer at random, unable to immediately recall the specific letter that was the source of their anxiety.
output: Such a conclusion could not pass unanswered by Mrs. Weston. She thought well of Frank in almost every respect; and, what was more, she loved him very much, and her defence was, therefore, earnest. She talked with a great deal of reason, and at least equal affection - but she had too much to urge for Emma’s attention; it was soon gone to Brunswick Square or to Donwell; she forgot to attempt to listen; and when Mrs. Weston ended with, “We have not yet had the letter we are so anxious for, you know, but I hope it will soon come,” she was obliged to pause before she answered, and at last obliged to answer at random, before she could at all recollect what letter it was which they were so anxious for.
title: Emma
author: Jane Austen

input: Mr. Weston's happiness was clear and unmistakable. He was truly delighted, as this was exactly the situation he had hoped for. Now Frank would genuinely be part of their neighborhood. After all, what did nine miles mean to a young man? Just an hour's ride. He would be able to visit constantly. The difference between Richmond and London in this regard was enough to determine whether they would see him regularly or not at all. Sixteen miles—or even eighteen, since it was a full eighteen to Manchester Street—was a serious obstacle. Even if he managed to get away, the entire day would be consumed by traveling there and back. There was no comfort in having him in London; he might as well be at Enscombe. Richmond, however, was exactly the right distance for easy visits. This suggests that closer was not necessarily better.
output: Mr. Weston’s own happiness was indisputable. He was quite delighted. It was the very circumstance he could have wished for. Now, it would be really having Frank in their neighbourhood. What were nine miles to a young man? - An hour’s ride. He would be always coming over. The difference in that respect of Richmond and London was enough to make the whole difference of seeing him always and seeing him never. Sixteen miles - nay, eighteen - it must be full eighteen to Manchester-street - was a serious obstacle. Were he ever able to get away, the day would be spent in coming and returning. There was no comfort in having him in London; he might as well be at Enscombe; but Richmond was the very distance for easy intercourse. Better than nearer!
title: Emma
author: Jane Austen

input: “A man,” he remarked, “must possess a significantly high opinion of himself when he invites others to leave the comfort of their own fireside to face a day such as this for the purpose of visiting him. He must believe himself to be a most agreeable individual; I could not undertake such an action. It is the utmost absurdity—indeed, it is presently snowing!—to insist that individuals forsake their comfort at home, as well as the folly of individuals not choosing to remain comfortably at home when they have the opportunity to do so. If we were compelled to venture out on an evening like this due to any obligation or necessity, we would consider it a considerable hardship; yet here we are, likely clad in somewhat lighter garments than usual, proceeding voluntarily, without justification, in defiance of the instinct of nature, which advises humanity, through every sensory experience, to remain at home and shelter what they can. Here we are, preparing to spend five tedious hours in another individual’s residence, with nothing to discuss or hear that has not already been exchanged yesterday and may not be repeated tomorrow. We are venturing out in dismal weather, with the prospect of returning in even worse conditions; four horses and four servants have been summoned merely to transport five idle, shivering individuals into colder rooms and inferior company than they could have enjoyed at home.”
output: “A man,” said he, “must have a very good opinion of himself when he asks people to leave their own fireside, and encounter such a day as this, for the sake of coming to see him. He must think himself a most agreeable fellow; I could not do such a thing. It is the greatest absurdity - Actually snowing at this moment! - The folly of not allowing people to be comfortable at home - and the folly of people’s not staying comfortably at home when they can! If we were obliged to go out such an evening as this, by any call of duty or business, what a hardship we should deem it; - and here are we, probably with rather thinner clothing than usual, setting forward voluntarily, without excuse, in defiance of the voice of nature, which tells man, in every thing given to his view or his feelings, to stay at home himself, and keep all under shelter that he can; - here are we setting forward to spend five dull hours in another man’s house, with nothing to say or to hear that was not said and heard yesterday, and may not be said and heard again to-morrow. Going in dismal weather, to return probably in worse; - four horses and four servants taken out for nothing but to convey five idle, shivering creatures into colder rooms and worse company than they might have had at home.”
title: Emma
author: Jane Austen

input:
After Mr. and Mrs. Darling departed the house, the night-lights beside the beds of the three children continued to glow brightly. They were particularly charming night-lights, and one might wish that the children could have stayed awake to see Peter. However, Wendy's light flickered and emitted a large yawn, which caused the other two lights to yawn as well. Before they could manage to stop, all three lights extinguished.

Now, a new light filled the room, a thousand times more brilliant than the night-lights. During the time it took to describe this, it had searched through all the drawers in the nursery, seeking Peter's shadow, rummaged through the wardrobe, and turned every pocket inside out. This was not a traditional light; it created illumination by moving rapidly. When it paused for a moment, one could see it was a fairy, no larger than a hand, yet still growing. Her name was Tinker Bell, and she was elegantly dressed in a skeleton leaf, tailored to showcase her figure effectively. She had a slight tendency toward being plump.
output:
For a moment after Mr. and Mrs. Darling left the house the night-lights by the beds of the three children continued to burn clearly. They were awfully nice little night-lights, and one cannot help wishing that they could have kept awake to see Peter; but Wendy’s light blinked and gave such a yawn that the other two yawned also, and before they could close their mouths all the three went out.

There was another light in the room now, a thousand times brighter than the night-lights, and in the time we have taken to say this, it had been in all the drawers in the nursery, looking for Peter’s shadow, rummaged the wardrobe and turned every pocket inside out. It was not really a light; it made this light by flashing about so quickly, but when it came to rest for a second you saw it was a fairy, no longer than your hand, but still growing. It was a girl called Tinker Bell exquisitely gowned in a skeleton leaf, cut low and square, through which her figure could be seen to the best advantage. She was slightly inclined to embonpoint.
title: Peter Pan
author: J. M. Barrie

input: Michael expressed his refusal in a playful manner, prompting Mrs. Darling to leave the room to retrieve a chocolate treat for him. Mr. Darling interpreted this action as a lack of discipline. This reflects his genuine belief in the importance of firmness in parenting. Wendy, now dressed for bed, supported Michael by suggesting that the medicine their father occasionally takes is even more unpleasant. Meanwhile, Mr. Darling had not truly discarded the medicine; instead, he had secretly placed it at the top of the wardrobe during the night. Unbeknownst to him, Liza, the devoted servant, had discovered the medicine and returned it to its usual spot on his wash-stand.
output:
“Won’t; won’t!” Michael cried naughtily. Mrs. Darling left the room to get a chocolate for him, and Mr. Darling thought this showed want of firmness.

He really thought this was true, and Wendy, who was now in her night-gown, believed it also, and she said, to encourage Michael, “That medicine you sometimes take, father, is much nastier, isn’t it?”

He had not exactly lost it; he had climbed in the dead of night to the top of the wardrobe and hidden it there. What he did not know was that the faithful Liza had found it, and put it back on his wash-stand.
title: Peter Pan
author: J. M. Barrie

The blow has always fallen at the end of the time it would take the senders to travel the distance. However, this one comes from London, so we cannot count on any delay.

The papers Openshaw carried are clearly of vital importance to the person or persons on the sailing ship. I think it is quite clear that there must be more than one of them. A single man could not have carried out two deaths in a way that would deceive a coroner's jury. There must have been several involved, and they must have been men of resource and determination. output:
“More than that. It is probable. And now you see the deadly urgency of this new case, and why I urged young Openshaw to caution. The blow has always fallen at the end of the time which it would take the senders to travel the distance. But this one comes from London, and therefore we cannot count upon delay.”

“The papers which Openshaw carried are obviously of vital importance to the person or persons in the sailing-ship. I think that it is quite clear that there must be more than one of them. A single man could not have carried out two deaths in such a way as to deceive a coroner’s jury. There must have been several in it, and they must have been men of resource and determination. Their papers they mean to have, be the holder of them who it may. In this way you see K. K. K. ceases to be the initials of an individual and becomes the badge of a society.”
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input:
We heard the door open, followed by a brief conversation and rapid footsteps on the linoleum. Then, our own door opened and a woman, dressed in dark clothing and wearing a black veil, entered the room. This highlights the urgency of the situation. The woman was greeted warmly and offered refreshments, with the suggestion that she sit comfortably and share her story. It was also proposed that James be sent to bed, if that would be preferable. 

This suggests that the woman had spoken to us about her husband's issues before, seeking both medical and emotional support. As a doctor, I had previously discussed her husband's trouble with her, while my wife had offered comfort as an old friend and school companion. We responded with supportive words, attempting to soothe and comfort her. Ultimately, our conversation turned to the question of her husband's whereabouts and the possibility of his return. We asked if she knew where he was and whether it might be possible to bring him back to her.
output:
We heard the door open, a few hurried words, and then quick steps upon the linoleum. Our own door flew open, and a lady, clad in some dark-coloured stuff, with a black veil, entered the room.

“It was very sweet of you to come. Now, you must have some wine and water, and sit here comfortably and tell us all about it. Or should you rather that I sent James off to bed?”

It was not the first time that she had spoken to us of her husband’s trouble, to me as a doctor, to my wife as an old friend and school companion. We soothed and comforted her by such words as we could find. Did she know where her husband was? Was it possible that we could bring him back to her?
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input: I had somewhat overlooked the unusual pets that the Doctor seemed to favor. There was also a cheetah, which might appear at any moment, resting on our shoulders. I must admit that I felt more at ease after following Holmes’ lead and taking off my shoes as I stepped into the bedroom. My companion quietly closed the shutters, placed the lamp on the table, and surveyed the room. Everything appeared as it had during the day. Then, approaching me and cupping his hand to form a makeshift trumpet, he softly whispered into my ear, so gently that I struggled to catch his words.
output: I had forgotten the strange pets which the Doctor affected. There was a cheetah, too; perhaps we might find it upon our shoulders at any moment. I confess that I felt easier in my mind when, after following Holmes’ example and slipping off my shoes, I found myself inside the bedroom. My companion noiselessly closed the shutters, moved the lamp onto the table, and cast his eyes round the room. All was as we had seen it in the daytime. Then creeping up to me and making a trumpet of his hand, he whispered into my ear again so gently that it was all that I could do to distinguish the words:
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input: Holmes paused at the corner to observe the line of houses. He expressed his interest in memorizing their order, as he enjoys having an accurate knowledge of London. He noted the locations of Mortimer’s tobacconist, a small newspaper shop, the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank, the Vegetarian Restaurant, and McFarlane’s carriage-building depot, which marked the end of that block. He then turned to Doctor and suggested that they had completed their work for the day and it was time to enjoy some leisure. He proposed they have a sandwich and a cup of coffee before heading to a concert, a place associated with beauty, delicacy, and harmony, free from the complications posed by challenging clients.
output: “Let me see,” said Holmes, standing at the corner and glancing along the line, “I should like just to remember the order of the houses here. It is a hobby of mine to have an exact knowledge of London. There is Mortimer’s, the tobacconist, the little newspaper shop, the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank, the Vegetarian Restaurant, and McFarlane’s carriage-building depot. That carries us right on to the other block. And now, Doctor, we’ve done our work, so it’s time we had some play. A sandwich and a cup of coffee, and then off to violin-land, where all is sweetness and delicacy and harmony, and there are no red-headed clients to vex us with their conundrums.”
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input:
A young boy presented two books, one small and thin, the other large and greasy, placing them together beneath the lamp. Sherlock Holmes appeared visibly upset. He took a sovereign from his pocket and placed it on the table, turning away as if his discontent was too profound for expression. A few moments later, he paused under a lamp-post and laughed in a silent manner characteristic of him.

He noted that a man with distinctive whiskers and the "Pink ’un" newspaper visible from his pocket could easily be persuaded to share information through a wager. He suggested that if he had offered the man £100 directly, he would not have provided as thorough information as he did when prompted by the notion of a bet. Holmes then indicated that they were likely close to concluding their investigation, with only the decision remaining about whether to visit Mrs. Oakshott that evening or to postpone until the following day. He observed that the response from the unfriendly man implied that there were others, in addition to themselves, who were concerned about the situation.
output:
The small boy brought round a small thin volume and a great greasy-backed one, laying them out together beneath the hanging lamp.

Sherlock Holmes looked deeply chagrined. He drew a sovereign from his pocket and threw it down upon the slab, turning away with the air of a man whose disgust is too deep for words. A few yards off he stopped under a lamp-post and laughed in the hearty, noiseless fashion which was peculiar to him.

“When you see a man with whiskers of that cut and the ‘Pink ’un’ protruding out of his pocket, you can always draw him by a bet,” said he. “I daresay that if I had put £ 100 down in front of him, that man would not have given me such complete information as was drawn from him by the idea that he was doing me on a wager. Well, Watson, we are, I fancy, nearing the end of our quest, and the only point which remains to be determined is whether we should go on to this Mrs. Oakshott to-night, or whether we should reserve it for to-morrow. It is clear from what that surly fellow said that there are others besides ourselves who are anxious about the matter, and I should - ”
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input:
The young man retrieved a crumpled envelope from his waistcoat and carefully poured five small dried orange pips onto the table. 

"To tell the truth," he said, lowering his face into his thin, white hands, "I have felt helpless. I feel like one of those unfortunate rabbits when a snake approaches. I appear to be caught in the hold of some relentless, inevitable evil, which no amount of foresight or precautions can protect me from."
output:
The young man took from his waistcoat a crumpled envelope, and turning to the table he shook out upon it five little dried orange pips.

“To tell the truth” - he sank his face into his thin, white hands - “I have felt helpless. I have felt like one of those poor rabbits when the snake is writhing towards it. I seem to be in the grasp of some resistless, inexorable evil, which no foresight and no precautions can guard against.”
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input:
We will strive to clarify these matters for you. First, I would like to ask you a few questions, Mr. Wilson. How long has your assistant, who initially drew your attention to the advertisement, been working with you? 

He is small, stout, and very quick in his movements. He has no facial hair, despite being over thirty years old. There is a white mark on his forehead caused by acid.

Holmes sat up in his chair, clearly excited. He remarked, “I suspected as much. Have you ever noticed that his ears are pierced for earrings?”
output:
“We shall endeavour to clear up these points for you. And, first, one or two questions, Mr. Wilson. This assistant of yours who first called your attention to the advertisement - how long had he been with you?”

“Small, stout-built, very quick in his ways, no hair on his face, though he’s not short of thirty. Has a white splash of acid upon his forehead.”

Holmes sat up in his chair in considerable excitement. “I thought as much,” said he. “Have you ever observed that his ears are pierced for earrings?”
title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input: Additionally, human beings exhibit a propensity for timidity and apology, having abandoned an upright posture; they no longer dare to express their thoughts or assert their existence without referencing the opinions of revered individuals. Furthermore, they experience feelings of shame in the presence of even the most mundane aspects of the natural world, such as a blade of grass or a rose in bloom. It is worth noting that the roses situated beneath my window do not draw comparisons with previous or supposedly superior roses; instead, they exist solely for their present purpose, coexisting with a higher power in the current moment. Moreover, these roses are not bound by temporal constraints, for they are perfect and self-sufficient in every instant of their existence. In essence, the entire life cycle of a rose is inherently contained within each stage of its development, from the initial leaf-bud to the fully bloomed flower, and ultimately to the leafless root, with no aspect being more or less significant than any other. The nature of the rose is thus fulfilled, and it, in turn, fulfills the natural order, in a state of equilibrium that persists throughout all moments. However, human beings tend to postpone or reminisce, failing to live in the present, instead lamenting the past or anxiously anticipating the future, oblivious to the abundant resources that surround them. It is worth noting that humans cannot attain happiness and strength until they learn to coexist with nature in the present, transcending the limitations of time.
output: Man is timid and apologetic; he is no longer upright; he dares not say "I think," "I am," but quotes some saint or sage. He is ashamed before the blade of grass or the blowing rose. These roses under my window make no reference to former roses or to better ones; they are for what they are; they exist with God to-day. There is no time to them. There is simply the rose; it is perfect in every moment of its existence. Before a leaf-bud has burst, its whole life acts; in the full-blown flower there is no more; in the leafless root there is no less. Its nature is satisfied, and it satisfies nature, in all moments alike. But man postpones, or remembers; he does not live in the present, but with a reverted eye laments the past, or, heedless of the riches that surround him, stands on tiptoe to foresee the future. He cannot be happy and strong until he too lives with nature in the present, above time.
title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

input: You may find yourself admiring this tower of granite, which has withstood the challenges of many ages. However, it is worth considering that this impressive structure was constructed by a small, skilled hand, suggesting that the creator may hold more significance than the creation itself. The hand that built the tower can often dismantle it even more swiftly. Perhaps more important than the hand is the unseen thought that guided its construction; behind every rough outcome, there tends to be a finer cause. When examined closely, what we perceive as permanent might reveal its underlying secrets. For instance, a considerable estate might seem like a solid and enduring fact to women and children, yet to a merchant, it may appear as something easily formed from various materials and just as easily lost. An orchard, well-tended land, and favorable conditions may seem like fixed assets to a city dweller, but to a larger farmer, they are often as changeable as the harvest. Nature may give the impression of stability, but it too has causes that can be understood, leading one to question whether these expansive fields and distinctive leaves truly remain so unchanging. The concept of permanence can vary in meaning. Everything exists in a state of flux. Just as moons do not limit spiritual power, neither do other tangible objects.
output: You admire this tower of granite, weathering the hurts of so many ages. Yet a little waving hand built this huge wall, and that which builds is better than that which is built. The hand that built can topple it down much faster. Better than the hand and nimbler was the invisible thought which wrought through it; and thus ever, behind the coarse effect, is a fine cause, which, being narrowly seen, is itself the effect of a finer cause. Everything looks permanent until its secret is known. A rich estate appears to women and children a firm and lasting fact; to a merchant, one easily created out of any materials, and easily lost. An orchard, good tillage, good grounds, seem a fixture, like a gold mine, or a river, to a citizen; but to a large farmer, not much more fixed than the state of the crop. Nature looks provokingly stable and secular, but it has a cause like all the rest; and when once I comprehend that, will these fields stretch so immovably wide, these leaves hang so individually considerable? Permanence is a word of degrees. Every thing is medial. Moons are no more bounds to spiritual power than bat-balls.
title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

input: People may think that when you reject popular standards, you are rejecting all standards and simply embracing lawlessness; and a bold, pleasure-seeking person may use the name of philosophy to make his crimes seem respectable. But the law of consciousness remains. There are two confessionals, and in one or the other we must be absolved. You may complete your round of duties by clearing yourself in the direct way or in the reflective way. Consider whether you have satisfied your relations to father, mother, cousin, neighbor, town, cat, and dog; whether any of these can rightly blame you. But I may also neglect this reflective standard and absolve myself to myself. I have my own strict claims and my own complete circle. It denies the name of duty to many offices that are called duties. Yet if I can pay its debts, it allows me to dispense with the popular code. If anyone imagines that this law is lax, let him keep its commandment for one day. In short, while others may mistake self-rule for lawlessness, the law of consciousness still holds, and it can either replace or confirm the ordinary code depending on how faithfully we meet its demands.
output: The populace think that your rejection of popular standards is a rejection of all standard, and mere antinomianism; and the bold sensualist will use the name of philosophy to gild his crimes. But the law of consciousness abides. There are two confessionals, in one or the other of which we must be shriven. You may fulfill your round of duties by clearing yourself in the direct, or in the reflex way. Consider whether you have satisfied your relations to father, mother, cousin, neighbor, town, cat, and dog; whether any of these can upbraid you. But I may also neglect this reflex standard, and absolve me to myself. I have my own stern claims and perfect circle. It denies the name of duty to many offices that are called duties. But if I can discharge its debts, it enables me to dispense with the popular code. If any one imagines that this law is lax, let him keep its commandment one day.
title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

input: We require books that possess this profound cathartic quality far more than we require books focused on political science or private economics. Life presents itself as a celebration solely to the wise. When viewed from the perspective of prudence, it reveals a tattered and perilous facade. The transgressions against the laws of nature committed by both our predecessors and contemporaries result in consequences that affect us as well. The presence of disease and deformity in our environment serves as a testament to the violations of natural, intellectual, and moral laws, often compounding these violations to generate pervasive suffering. Conditions such as tetanus that contorts an individual’s posture, rabies that induces irrational behavior towards loved ones, and madness that leads to bizarre eating habits—along with war, plague, cholera, and famine—reflect a certain brutality inherent in nature. This brutality, having originated from human wrongdoing, must manifest itself through human suffering. Unfortunately, it is noteworthy that nearly every individual has, to some degree, become a participant in this collective wrongdoing, thereby rendering themselves liable for a share in the subsequent atonement.
output: 3. We need books of this tart cathartic virtue, more than books of political science, or of private economy. Life is a festival only to the wise. Seen from the nook and chimney-side of prudence, it wears a ragged and dangerous front. The violations of the laws of nature by our predecessors and our contemporaries are punished in us also. The disease and deformity around us certify the infraction of natural, intellectual, and moral laws, and often violation on violation to breed such compound misery. A lockjaw that bends a man's head back to his heels, hydrophobia that makes him bark at his wife and babes, insanity that makes him eat grass; war, plague, cholera, famine indicate a certain ferocity in nature, which, as it had its inlet by human crime, must have its outlet by human suffering. Unhappily, almost no man exists who has not in his own person become, to some amount, a stockholder in the sin, and so made himself liable to a share in the expiation.
title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

input:
Upon arriving home, he noticed that his servant was still awake, waiting for him. He instructed the servant to rest and then settled onto the sofa in the library, reflecting on some of the remarks made by Lord Henry. 

He began to question whether it was indeed true that one could never change. A deep yearning for the innocence of his youth surfaced—his pure, unblemished boyhood, as Lord Henry had referred to it. He was aware that he had compromised himself, allowing corruption to infiltrate his thoughts and instilling a sense of horror in his imagination; he recognized that he had negatively influenced others and had taken a troubling pleasure in doing so. Among the lives he had interacted with, it was those with the greatest potential that he had led to disappointment. Yet, he wondered if all was lost. Was there no possibility for redemption?
output:
When he reached home, he found his servant waiting up for him. He sent him to bed, and threw himself down on the sofa in the library, and began to think over some of the things that Lord Henry had said to him.

Was it really true that one could never change? He felt a wild longing for the unstained purity of his boyhood - his rose-white boyhood, as Lord Henry had once called it. He knew that he had tarnished himself, filled his mind with corruption and given horror to his fancy; that he had been an evil influence to others, and had experienced a terrible joy in being so; and that of the lives that had crossed his own, it had been the fairest and the most full of promise that he had brought to shame. But was it all irretrievable? Was there no hope for him?
title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde

input: The worship of the senses has often been criticized, as many people instinctively fear passions and sensations that seem more powerful than themselves, sensations shared with less complex forms of life. However, Dorian Gray believed that the true essence of the senses had not been fully grasped. He thought they had remained primitive and animalistic because society attempted to suppress or punish them, rather than nurturing them as components of a new spirituality characterized by an appreciation for beauty. Reflecting on humanity's journey through history, he felt a profound sense of loss. Much had been sacrificed with little benefit, leading to extreme rejection of pleasure and painful self-denial. These responses stemmed from fear and resulted in a degradation that was far worse than the imagined decline they sought to avoid. Nature, in its ironic way, drove the ascetic into the wild, providing him with animals as companions instead of fellow humans.
output: The worship of the senses has often, and with much justice, been decried, men feeling a natural instinct of terror about passions and sensations that seem stronger than themselves, and that they are conscious of sharing with the less highly organized forms of existence. But it appeared to Dorian Gray that the true nature of the senses had never been understood, and that they had remained savage and animal merely because the world had sought to starve them into submission or to kill them by pain, instead of aiming at making them elements of a new spirituality, of which a fine instinct for beauty was to be the dominant characteristic. As he looked back upon man moving through history, he was haunted by a feeling of loss. So much had been surrendered! and to such little purpose! There had been mad wilful rejections, monstrous forms of self-torture and self-denial, whose origin was fear and whose result was a degradation infinitely more terrible than that fancied degradation from which, in their ignorance, they had sought to escape; Nature, in her wonderful irony, driving out the anchorite to feed with the wild animals of the desert and giving to the hermit the beasts of the field as his companions.
title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde

input:
"Your life seems quite troubling, full of challenges that may have led you down a difficult path. It appears that your journey has culminated in some serious decisions. As I consider my next steps, it’s not your life that occupies my thoughts."

"Ah, Alan," Dorian replied softly with a sigh, "I wish you could feel even a small fraction of the compassion for me that I feel for you." He then turned his gaze toward the garden. Campbell remained silent in response.
output:
“Your life? Good heavens! what a life that is! You have gone from corruption to corruption, and now you have culminated in crime. In doing what I am going to do - what you force me to do - it is not of your life that I am thinking.”

“Ah, Alan,” murmured Dorian with a sigh, “I wish you had a thousandth part of the pity for me that I have for you.” He turned away as he spoke and stood looking out at the garden. Campbell made no answer.
title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde

input:
When a highly respected physician, who also happens to be one's husband, tells friends and family that there is likely nothing wrong except for a temporary bout of nervous depression and a minor tendency toward hysteria, it leaves one in a difficult position. 

My brother, who is also a physician of similar reputation, shares the same opinion.

As a result, I am advised to take phosphates or phosphites—whichever it may be—along with tonics, travel, fresh air, and exercise, while being strongly discouraged from engaging in any work until I feel better. In summary, the situation involves navigating the recommendations of trusted medical professionals while managing personal health concerns.
output:
If a physician of high standing, and one’s own husband, assures friends and relatives that there is really nothing the matter with one but temporary nervous depression - a slight hysterical tendency - what is one to do?

My brother is also a physician, and also of high standing, and he says the same thing.

So I take phosphates or phosphites - whichever it is, and tonics, and journeys, and air, and exercise, and am absolutely forbidden to “work” until I am well again.
title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
It is rare for ordinary individuals such as John and me to acquire ancestral homes for the summer. 

A colonial mansion, a hereditary estate, or even a haunted house would be a delightful notion, yet that may be too much to hope for. 

If it were not, why would it be rented at such a low price? Additionally, why has it remained unoccupied for so long? 

John is exceedingly practical. He lacks patience for faith, harbors a strong aversion to superstition, and openly mocks any discussions of concepts that cannot be experienced through the senses or quantified.
output:
It is very seldom that mere ordinary people like John and myself secure ancestral halls for the summer.

A colonial mansion, a hereditary estate, I would say a haunted house, and reach the height of romantic felicity - but that would be asking too much of fate!

Else, why should it be let so cheaply? And why have stood so long untenanted?

John is practical in the extreme. He has no patience with faith, an intense horror of superstition, and he scoffs openly at any talk of things not to be felt and seen and put down in figures.
title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
John has never seemed nervous in his life. He finds amusement in my reaction to the wallpaper. 

Initially, he planned to replace it, but later he suggested that I was allowing it to dominate my thoughts. He asserted that for someone with a nervous disposition, indulging such whims is detrimental.

He explained that if the wallpaper were removed, I would then focus on the heavy bedstead, followed by the barred windows, and ultimately the gate at the top of the stairs, and so forth.
output:
I suppose John never was nervous in his life. He laughs at me so about this wallpaper!

At first he meant to repaper the room, but afterwards he said that I was letting it get the better of me, and that nothing was worse for a nervous patient than to give way to such fancies.

He said that after the wallpaper was changed it would be the heavy bedstead, and then the barred windows, and then that gate at the head of the stairs, and so on.
title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input: As we prepared to sign the aforementioned articles, which would bind us and our heirs for fifty years, Mr. Brockden, the scrivener, addressed us. He noted, "You are young men, but it is unlikely that any of you will live to see the end of the term established in the document." Despite his assertion, several of us are still living today. However, the instrument was rendered void just a few years later due to a charter that incorporated the company and granted it perpetual status.
output: When we were about to sign the above mentioned articles, which were to be binding on us, our heirs, etc., for fifty years, Mr. Brockden, the scrivener, said to us, "You are young men, but it is scarcely probable that any of you will live to see the expiration of the term fix'd in the instrument." A number of us, however, are yet living; but the instrument was after a few years rendered null by a charter that incorporated and gave perpetuity to the company.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Mr. Logan, who adhered to the Quaker faith, wrote an address in support of defensive war, providing several strong arguments for his stance. He entrusted me with sixty pounds to be invested in lottery tickets for the battery, with instructions for any prizes to be dedicated solely to that purpose. He shared an anecdote about his former employer, William Penn, regarding the topic of defense. As a young man, Penn traveled from England with his proprietary and served as their secretary during a time of war. Their ship was pursued by an armed vessel believed to be an enemy. The captain prepared for defense but informed Penn and the Quakers that their assistance was not anticipated, encouraging them to retreat to the cabin. However, James Logan chose to remain on deck and took his position by a gun. Ultimately, the supposed enemy turned out to be an ally, and no conflict ensued. When Logan returned below deck to share this information, Penn reprimanded him for remaining on deck and participating in defense, citing the principles of Friends and that such action had not been requested by the captain. This rebuke, delivered in front of others, irritated Logan, who responded, "As your servant, why did you not command me to come down? It seemed you were content for me to help defend the ship when you perceived danger."
output: The honorable and learned Mr. Logan, who had always been of that sect, was one who wrote an address to them, declaring his approbation of defensive war, and supporting his opinion by many strong arguments. He put into my hands sixty pounds to be laid out in lottery tickets for the battery, with directions to apply what prizes might be drawn wholly to that service. He told me the following anecdote of his old master, William Penn, respecting defense. He came over from England, when a young man, with that proprietary, and as his secretary. It was war-time, and their ship was chas'd by an armed vessel, suppos'd to be an enemy. Their captain prepar'd for defense; but told William Penn, and his company of Quakers, that he did not expect their assistance, and they might retire into the cabin, which they did, except James Logan, who chose to stay upon deck, and was quarter'd to a gun. The suppos'd enemy prov'd a friend, so there was no fighting; but when the secretary went down to communicate the intelligence, William Penn rebuk'd him severely for staying upon deck, and undertaking to assist in defending the vessel, contrary to the principles of Friends, especially as it had not been required by the captain. This reproof, being before all the company, piqu'd the secretary, who answer'd, "I being thy servant, why did thee not order me to come down? But thee was willing enough that I should stay and help to fight the ship when thee thought there was danger."
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: I stayed there for nearly three months, and by that time I could count among my new friends Judge Allen, Samuel Bustill, the secretary of the Province, Isaac Pearson, Joseph Cooper, and several members of the Smith family who were in the Assembly, as well as Isaac Decow, the surveyor-general. The latter was a shrewd and wise old man who told me that he had started out on his own when he was young by hauling clay for brick-makers, learned to write after he had reached adulthood, carried the chain for surveyors who then taught him surveying, and had now, through his own hard work, acquired a comfortable estate. He said to me, "I foresee that you will soon take this man's business away from him and make a fortune in it at Philadelphia." At that time he had no idea at all that I intended to set up there or anywhere else. These friends were later very helpful to me, just as I was occasionally helpful to some of them, and they all continued to think well of me for as long as they lived.
output: We continu'd there near three months; and by that time I could reckon among my acquired friends, Judge Allen, Samuel Bustill, the secretary of the Province, Isaac Pearson, Joseph Cooper, and several of the Smiths, members of Assembly, and Isaac Decow, the surveyor-general. The latter was a shrewd, sagacious old man, who told me that he began for himself, when young, by wheeling clay for brick-makers, learned to write after he was of age, carri'd the chain for surveyors, who taught him surveying, and he had now by his industry, acquir'd a good estate; and says he, "I foresee that you will soon work this man out of his business, and make a fortune in it at Philadelphia." He had not then the least intimation of my intention to set up there or anywhere. These friends were afterwards of great use to me, as I occasionally was to some of them. They all continued their regard for me as long as they lived.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input:
A journey to New England was undertaken this year due to post-office business, during which the College of Cambridge conferred upon me the degree of Master of Arts. This highlights the fact that I received this honor without having studied at any college. Previously, Yale College in Connecticut had also awarded me a similar degree, in recognition of my contributions to the field of electricity in natural philosophy. 

The prospect of war with France in 1754 led to the organization of a congress of commissioners from various colonies, as ordered by the Lords of Trade. This congress was to assemble at Albany to discuss defense strategies with the chiefs of the Six Nations, aiming to protect both their territory and ours. Governor Hamilton informed the House of this development and requested that they provide suitable gifts for the Indian leaders. He also nominated the speaker, Mr. Norris, and myself, along with Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters, to serve as commissioners for Pennsylvania. The House approved these nominations and supplied the necessary goods for the gifts, although they were not entirely enthusiastic about conducting negotiations outside of the province. Ultimately, we met with the other commissioners at Albany in mid-June. This suggests that the colonies were taking steps to coordinate their efforts and build alliances in preparation for potential conflict.
output:
The business of the post-office occasion'd my taking a journey this year to New England, where the College of Cambridge, of their own motion, presented me with the degree of Master of Arts. Yale College, in Connecticut, had before made me a similar compliment. Thus, without studying in any college, I came to partake of their honours. They were conferr'd in consideration of my improvements and discoveries in the electric branch of natural philosophy.

In 1754, war with France being again apprehended, a congress of commissioners from the different colonies was, by an order of the Lords of Trade, to be assembled at Albany, there to confer with the chiefs of the Six Nations concerning the means of defending both their country and ours. Governor Hamilton, having receiv'd this order, acquainted the House with it, requesting they would furnish proper presents for the Indians, to be given on this occasion; and naming the speaker (Mr. Norris) and myself to join Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters as commissioners to act for Pennsylvania. The House approv'd the nomination, and provided the goods for the present, and tho' they did not much like treating out of the provinces; and we met the other commissioners at Albany about the middle of June.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Additionally, it appears that certain individuals perceive the entirety of human existence as having been thoroughly explored by their predecessors, with all aspects of life, including both the most elevated and the most mundane, having been carefully considered. Furthermore, according to Evelyn, historical figures such as Solomon and the Roman prætors have established guidelines for various aspects of life, including the placement of trees and the frequency with which one may enter a neighbor's property to collect items that have fallen onto it. Moreover, prominent figures like Hippocrates have even provided instructions on seemingly trivial matters, such as the proper method for cutting one's nails, which, in this case, is to trim them to a length that is even with the tips of the fingers. In essence, the feelings of tedium and ennui that arenote to have exhausted the diversity and pleasures of life are, in fact, as ancient as humanity itself. It is worth noting that human capabilities have never been fully assessed, and it is unwise to evaluate an individual's potential based on past achievements, given that so little has been attempted. Moreover, regardless of any past failures, it is advisable not to be disheartened, for it is impossible to determine what tasks remain unaccomplished, and thus, one should not be unduly troubled by unfulfilled potential.
output: The whole ground of human life seems to some to have been gone over by their predecessors, both the heights and the valleys, and all things to have been cared for. According to Evelyn, “the wise Solomon prescribed ordinances for the very distances of trees; and the Roman prætors have decided how often you may go into your neighbor’s land to gather the acorns which fall on it without trespass, and what share belongs to that neighbor.” Hippocrates has even left directions how we should cut our nails; that is, even with the ends of the fingers, neither shorter nor longer. Undoubtedly the very tedium and ennui which presume to have exhausted the variety and the joys of life are as old as Adam. But man’s capacities have never been measured; nor are we to judge of what he can do by any precedents, so little has been tried. Whatever have been thy failures hitherto, “be not afflicted, my child, for who shall assign to thee what thou hast left undone?”
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: It is worth noting that my extensive engagement with beans constituted a unique experience, encompassing the processes of planting, hoeing, harvesting, threshing, and ultimately selling them; the latter task proved to be the most challenging of all, although I may add that tasting the beans also formed a part of my endeavor. My resolve to understand beans was unwavering. During their growth, I would hoe from five o’clock in the morning until noon and typically spent the remainder of the day attending to other responsibilities. Furthermore, one must consider the profound and intricate familiarity one develops with various types of weeds; this aspect merits some elaboration, as the labor involved was certainly repetitive. I ruthlessly disrupted their delicate structures, making stark distinctions with my hoe, leveling entire rows of one species while meticulously cultivating another. That is Roman wormwood; that is pigweed; that is sorrel; that is piper-grass—one must engage with them, sever their roots from the earth, exposing them to the sun, as any remaining fiber in the shade enables them to revert, becoming as verdant as a leek within two days. It was a prolonged struggle, not against cranes but rather against weeds, those persistent adversaries that enjoyed the advantages of sun, rain, and dew. Daily, the beans witnessed my arrival as I came to their defense, armed with a hoe, systematically thinning the ranks of their foes and filling the trenches with the fallen weeds. Many a formidable Hector, towering a full foot above his fellow competitors, succumbed to my efforts and lay defeated in the dust.
output: It was a singular experience that long acquaintance which I cultivated with beans, what with planting, and hoeing, and harvesting, and threshing, and picking over and selling them, - the last was the hardest of all, - I might add eating, for I did taste. I was determined to know beans. When they were growing, I used to hoe from five o’clock in the morning till noon, and commonly spent the rest of the day about other affairs. Consider the intimate and curious acquaintance one makes with various kinds of weeds, - it will bear some iteration in the account, for there was no little iteration in the labor, - disturbing their delicate organizations so ruthlessly, and making such invidious distinctions with his hoe, levelling whole ranks of one species, and sedulously cultivating another. That’s Roman wormwood, - that’s pigweed, - that’s sorrel, - that’s piper-grass, - have at him, chop him up, turn his roots upward to the sun, don’t let him have a fibre in the shade, if you do he’ll turn himself t’other side up and be as green as a leek in two days. A long war, not with cranes, but with weeds, those Trojans who had sun and rain and dews on their side. Daily the beans saw me come to their rescue armed with a hoe, and thin the ranks of their enemies, filling up the trenches with weedy dead. Many a lusty crest-waving Hector, that towered a whole foot above his crowding comrades, fell before my weapon and rolled in the dust.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
At midnight, when the moon was present, I would occasionally encounter hounds in my path as I walked through the woods. These animals would retreat from my way, seemingly fearful, and remain silent among the bushes until I had passed by. Meanwhile, squirrels and wild mice would compete for the store of nuts that I had accumulated. 

The area surrounding my house featured numerous pitch-pines, ranging in diameter from one to four inches, which had been damaged by mice during the previous winter. The winter had been particularly harsh for these animals, with deep snow covering the ground for an extended period, forcing them to incorporate a significant amount of pine bark into their diet. Nevertheless, by mid-summer, these trees appeared to be alive and thriving, with many of them having grown approximately one foot, despite being completely girdled. However, after enduring another winter, the girdled trees were invariably dead. It is noteworthy that a single mouse is able to consume an entire pine tree, gnawing around the trunk rather than up and down, and this phenomenon may be necessary to regulate the density of these trees, which tend to grow in close proximity to one another.
output:
At midnight, when there was a moon, I sometimes met with hounds in my path prowling about the woods, which would skulk out of my way, as if afraid, and stand silent amid the bushes till I had passed.

Squirrels and wild mice disputed for my store of nuts. There were scores of pitch-pines around my house, from one to four inches in diameter, which had been gnawed by mice the previous winter, - a Norwegian winter for them, for the snow lay long and deep, and they were obliged to mix a large proportion of pine bark with their other diet. These trees were alive and apparently flourishing at mid-summer, and many of them had grown a foot, though completely girdled; but after another winter such were without exception dead. It is remarkable that a single mouse should thus be allowed a whole pine tree for its dinner, gnawing round instead of up and down it; but perhaps it is necessary in order to thin these trees, which are wont to grow up densely.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: I observe the flow of morning cars with a sense of familiarity similar to that of watching the sun rise, which can often feel just as predictable. The trails of clouds stretching behind and ascending higher may briefly obscure the sun, casting my distant field into shadow, while the cars make their way to Boston. This celestial display can seem to diminish the significance of the earthly train of cars. The caretaker of the locomotive was up early on this winter morning, illuminated by starlight in the mountains, attending to his duties. Fire was stirred awake at this early hour to provide the necessary warmth and prepare the engine for its journey. If only the endeavor were as innocent as it is timely! When snow covers the ground, they may equip the engine with snow shoes and utilize a powerful plow to clear a path from the mountains to the coast, through which the cars, like a trailing drill, distribute restless passengers and goods across the nation. Throughout the day, the locomotive travels over the landscape, pausing only to allow its operator a rest. I sometimes find myself awakened at midnight by the engine’s heavy footsteps and forceful snorts, as it faces the harsh elements in a secluded forest, and it may only return to its station with the morning star, ready to embark on another journey without pause. Alternatively, I might hear it in the evening, releasing excess energy in its stable to relax before a few hours of rest. If only this endeavor were as noble and commanding as it is relentless and tireless!
output: I watch the passage of the morning cars with the same feeling that I do the rising of the sun, which is hardly more regular. Their train of clouds stretching far behind and rising higher and higher, going to heaven while the cars are going to Boston, conceals the sun for a minute and casts my distant field into the shade, a celestial train beside which the petty train of cars which hugs the earth is but the barb of the spear. The stabler of the iron horse was up early this winter morning by the light of the stars amid the mountains, to fodder and harness his steed. Fire, too, was awakened thus early to put the vital heat in him and get him off. If the enterprise were as innocent as it is early! If the snow lies deep, they strap on his snow-shoes, and with the giant plow, plow a furrow from the mountains to the seaboard, in which the cars, like a following drill-barrow, sprinkle all the restless men and floating merchandise in the country for seed. All day the fire-steed flies over the country, stopping only that his master may rest, and I am awakened by his tramp and defiant snort at midnight, when in some remote glen in the woods he fronts the elements incased in ice and snow; and he will reach his stall only with the morning star, to start once more on his travels without rest or slumber. Or perchance, at evening, I hear him in his stable blowing off the superfluous energy of the day, that he may calm his nerves and cool his liver and brain for a few hours of iron slumber. If the enterprise were as heroic and commanding as it is protracted and unwearied!
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: The indescribable innocence and benevolence of Nature, encompassing the sun, wind, and rain, as well as the seasons of summer and winter, provide an enduring sense of health and joy. Additionally, the deep connection that exists between Nature and humanity is so profound that, were any individual to experience genuine sorrow for justifiable reasons, the entirety of Nature would respond accordingly: the brightness of the sun would diminish, the winds would express a humane sigh, the clouds would weep, and the trees would shed their leaves, donning a veil of mourning even in the height of summer. It is worth noting that I seek to engage in a dialogue with the earth, pondering whether I am not, in part, composed of leaves and the very essence of the soil.
output: The indescribable innocence and beneficence of Nature, - of sun and wind and rain, of summer and winter, - such health, such cheer, they afford forever! and such sympathy have they ever with our race, that all Nature would be affected, and the sun’s brightness fade, and the winds would sigh humanely, and the clouds rain tears, and the woods shed their leaves and put on mourning in midsummer, if any man should ever for a just cause grieve. Shall I not have intelligence with the earth? Am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself?
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
The manager positioned himself beside the wheel, murmuring confidentially about the imperative of navigating well down the river before nightfall. It was at this moment that I observed a clearing in the distance along the riverside, accompanied by the outlines of what appeared to be a building. "What is this?" I inquired. He clapped his hands in amazement and exclaimed, "The station!" I immediately maneuvered the vessel closer while maintaining a cautious speed. 

Through my binoculars, I discerned the slope of a hill dotted with sparse trees, entirely devoid of undergrowth. A long, deteriorating structure atop the hill was partially obscured by tall grass; the expansive gaps in the peaked roof appeared dark from a distance. The surrounding jungle and woods formed a striking backdrop. There was an absence of any enclosure or fencing; however, it was evident that one had once existed, as I noted half a dozen slender posts remaining in a row near the house, each crudely trimmed and adorned with rounded carved balls at their upper ends. The rails or similar barriers that had previously connected them had vanished, enveloped by the encroaching forest. The riverbank remained clear, revealing a white man beneath a hat resembling a cart-wheel who was gesturing insistently with his entire arm. Upon scrutinizing the edges of the forest both above and below, I became increasingly convinced that I could perceive movements—human figures gliding discreetly to and fro. I proceeded past with caution, subsequently halting the engines to allow the vessel to drift downstream. The man on the shore began to call out, urging us to dock. "We have been attacked," the manager shouted in alarm. "I know—I know. It is all right," the other responded, his tone remarkably cheerful. "Come along. It is all right. I am glad."
output:
“The manager stood by the wheel murmuring confidentially about the necessity of getting well away down the river before dark at all events, when I saw in the distance a clearing on the riverside and the outlines of some sort of building. ‘What’s this?’ I asked. He clapped his hands in wonder. ‘The station!’ he cried. I edged in at once, still going half-speed.

“Through my glasses I saw the slope of a hill interspersed with rare trees and perfectly free from undergrowth. A long decaying building on the summit was half buried in the high grass; the large holes in the peaked roof gaped black from afar; the jungle and the woods made a background. There was no enclosure or fence of any kind; but there had been one apparently, for near the house half-a-dozen slim posts remained in a row, roughly trimmed, and with their upper ends ornamented with round carved balls. The rails, or whatever there had been between, had disappeared. Of course the forest surrounded all that. The river-bank was clear, and on the waterside I saw a white man under a hat like a cart-wheel beckoning persistently with his whole arm. Examining the edge of the forest above and below, I was almost certain I could see movements - human forms gliding here and there. I steamed past prudently, then stopped the engines and let her drift down. The man on the shore began to shout, urging us to land. ‘We have been attacked,’ screamed the manager. ‘I know - I know. It’s all right,’ yelled back the other, as cheerful as you please. ‘Come along. It’s all right. I am glad.’
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: His presence seemed to embody a profound darkness. I regarded him as one might observe someone at the bottom of a ravine where light rarely penetrates. However, my time to attend to him was limited, as I was assisting the engine driver in disassembling the leaking cylinders, straightening a bent connecting rod, and managing other similar tasks. My environment was often chaotic, filled with rust, metal shavings, nuts, bolts, wrenches, hammers, and ratchet drills—items I typically found challenging to work with. I looked after the small forge we were fortunate to have on board and labored diligently amidst what felt like a disorganized pile of scrap, unless my condition prevented me from standing. Overall, my efforts were focused on maintaining the machinery while navigating the difficulties of my surroundings.
output: “His was an impenetrable darkness. I looked at him as you peer down at a man who is lying at the bottom of a precipice where the sun never shines. But I had not much time to give him, because I was helping the engine-driver to take to pieces the leaky cylinders, to straighten a bent connecting-rod, and in other such matters. I lived in an infernal mess of rust, filings, nuts, bolts, spanners, hammers, ratchet-drills - things I abominate, because I don’t get on with them. I tended the little forge we fortunately had aboard; I toiled wearily in a wretched scrap-heap - unless I had the shakes too bad to stand.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: In essence, during my childhood, I harbored a profound fascination for maps. I would spend countless hours studying regions such as South America, Africa, and Australia, immersing myself in the wonders of exploration. At that time, there existed numerous blank spaces on the globe, and whenever I encountered a particularly enticing area on a map—though, in truth, all of them appeared inviting—I would place my finger on it and declare, “When I grow up, I shall travel there.” The North Pole was among these alluring destinations that I distinctly recall. However, I have yet to visit it and do not intend to pursue that aspiration now, as the allure has diminished. Furthermore, various other locations were scattered across the hemispheres. I have had the opportunity to visit some of those places, and the experiences are best left unexamined. Nevertheless, there remained one destination—the largest and most uncharted, so to speak—that I longed to explore.
output: “Now when I was a little chap I had a passion for maps. I would look for hours at South America, or Africa, or Australia, and lose myself in all the glories of exploration. At that time there were many blank spaces on the earth, and when I saw one that looked particularly inviting on a map (but they all look that) I would put my finger on it and say, ‘When I grow up I will go there.’ The North Pole was one of these places, I remember. Well, I haven’t been there yet, and shall not try now. The glamour’s off. Other places were scattered about the hemispheres. I have been in some of them, and... well, we won’t talk about that. But there was one yet - the biggest, the most blank, so to speak - that I had a hankering after.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: She extended her arms as if reaching for a departing figure, stretching them back with her pale hands clasped against the dimming light of the window. It may seem unlikely, but I could see him quite clearly at that moment. It seems that this poignant image will remain with me for as long as I live, and I may also remember her—a tragic and familiar presence—who, in this gesture, resembles another sorrowful figure adorned with powerless allure, reaching bare brown arms over the shimmering darkness of the stream. Then, in a soft voice, she remarked, "He died as he lived." This scene captures a blend of loss and remembrance.
output: “She put out her arms as if after a retreating figure, stretching them back and with clasped pale hands across the fading and narrow sheen of the window. Never see him! I saw him clearly enough then. I shall see this eloquent phantom as long as I live, and I shall see her, too, a tragic and familiar Shade, resembling in this gesture another one, tragic also, and bedecked with powerless charms, stretching bare brown arms over the glitter of the infernal stream, the stream of darkness. She said suddenly very low, ‘He died as he lived.’
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: I consider my departure from Colonel Lloyd's plantation to be one of the most significant events in my life. It is possible, and indeed quite likely, that had I not been relocated from that plantation to Baltimore, I would today find myself, rather than seated at my own table experiencing freedom and the joys of home while composing this narrative, in the distressing confines of slavery. The move to Baltimore established the foundation and opened the door to all my future successes. I have consistently viewed this event as the initial clear indication of that kind providence which has continuously accompanied me and enriched my life with numerous blessings. Furthermore, I found the selection of myself to be rather remarkable. There were several other enslaved children who could have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore, including those who were younger, those who were older, and those who were of a similar age. Ultimately, I was chosen from among them all, being the first, last, and sole selection.
output: I look upon my departure from Colonel Lloyd’s plantation as one of the most interesting events of my life. It is possible, and even quite probable, that but for the mere circumstance of being removed from that plantation to Baltimore, I should have to-day, instead of being here seated by my own table, in the enjoyment of freedom and the happiness of home, writing this Narrative, been confined in the galling chains of slavery. Going to live at Baltimore laid the foundation, and opened the gateway, to all my subsequent prosperity. I have ever regarded it as the first plain manifestation of that kind providence which has ever since attended me, and marked my life with so many favors. I regarded the selection of myself as being somewhat remarkable. There were a number of slave children that might have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore. There were those younger, those older, and those of the same age. I was chosen from among them all, and was the first, last, and only choice.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Colonel Lloyd's home plantation resembled a small country village, serving as the center for various mechanical operations for multiple farms. Tasks such as shoemaking, blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain grinding were all carried out by the enslaved individuals on this plantation. This environment had a distinctly business-like atmosphere, setting it apart from the neighboring farms. The plantation featured numerous houses, further enhancing its significance compared to others in the area. Known among the enslaved as the Great House Farm, being chosen to run errands there was highly valued by those on the outlying farms. This association with prestige elevated its status in their minds. A slave selected for errands at the Great House Farm felt a sense of pride comparable to a politician elected to the American Congress, as it represented the overseers' trust in them. This privilege was sought not only for the esteem it brought but also as an escape from the harsh conditions of fieldwork. The individual who received this honor frequently was regarded as the most capable and reliable, and competitors for this position worked hard to gain favor from their overseers, similar to how political candidates seek to win over the electorate. Such dynamics reveal parallels between the behavior of Colonel Lloyd's enslaved individuals and those involved in political life.
output: The home plantation of Colonel Lloyd wore the appearance of a country village. All the mechanical operations for all the farms were performed here. The shoemaking and mending, the blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain-grinding, were all performed by the slaves on the home plantation. The whole place wore a business-like aspect very unlike the neighboring farms. The number of houses, too, conspired to give it advantage over the neighboring farms. It was called by the slaves the Great House Farm. Few privileges were esteemed higher, by the slaves of the out-farms, than that of being selected to do errands at the Great House Farm. It was associated in their minds with greatness. A representative could not be prouder of his election to a seat in the American Congress, than a slave on one of the out-farms would be of his election to do errands at the Great House Farm. They regarded it as evidence of great confidence reposed in them by their overseers; and it was on this account, as well as a constant desire to be out of the field from under the driver’s lash, that they esteemed it a high privilege, one worth careful living for. He was called the smartest and most trusty fellow, who had this honor conferred upon him the most frequently. The competitors for this office sought as diligently to please their overseers, as the office-seekers in the political parties seek to please and deceive the people. The same traits of character might be seen in Colonel Lloyd’s slaves, as are seen in the slaves of the political parties.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Additionally, I resided with Mr. Covey for a period of one year. Furthermore, during the initial six months of that year, it is worth noting that scarcely a week elapsed without his subjecting me to corporal punishment. In essence, I was rarely devoid of physical discomfort, as a sore back was a persistent affliction. Moreover, my lack of dexterity and coordination was frequently cited by Mr. Covey as a justification for administering physical discipline. It is worth noting that our workload was maximized to the point of tolerability. Moreover, our daily routine commenced well before dawn, at which time we would attend to the needs of our horses and subsequently proceed to the field with our agricultural equipment. Additionally, Mr. Covey provided us with a sufficient quantity of food, albeit with limited time allocated for consumption. In many instances, our meals were rushed, with fewer than five minutes devoted to eating. Moreover, our workdays were often excessively long, frequently commencing at the earliest light of day and persisting until the last remnants of daylight had faded; and during periods of intense agricultural activity, such as the preservation of fodder, it was not uncommon for midnight to arrive while we were still engaged in our tasks, including the binding of harvested crops.
output: I lived with Mr. Covey one year. During the first six months, of that year, scarce a week passed without his whipping me. I was seldom free from a sore back. My awkwardness was almost always his excuse for whipping me. We were worked fully up to the point of endurance. Long before day we were up, our horses fed, and by the first approach of day we were off to the field with our hoes and ploughing teams. Mr. Covey gave us enough to eat, but scarce time to eat it. We were often less than five minutes taking our meals. We were often in the field from the first approach of day till its last lingering ray had left us; and at saving-fodder time, midnight often caught us in the field binding blades.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: This mode of treatment exemplifies the broader system of deception and cruelty associated with slavery. It highlights how the approach taken seeks to instill a revulsion toward freedom by exposing the enslaved individuals only to its negative aspects. A notable example is when a slave, who has a fondness for molasses, steals some. In many instances, the master then goes to town and purchases a large quantity. Upon returning, the master forces the slave to consume the molasses until he becomes sickened by it. This method is similarly applied to discourage slaves from requesting more food than their standard allowance. When a slave exhausts his ration and seeks additional food, the master often reacts with anger but, rather than sending the slave away hungry, provides an excessive amount and mandates consumption within a specific timeframe. If the slave then expresses difficulty in eating the food, he may be punished for being discontented, as he is deemed neither satisfied nor fasting. This suggests a broader pattern of punitive measures aimed at controlling the desires and actions of enslaved individuals. The examples provided illustrate a prevalent practice within this system.
output: I have said that this mode of treatment is a part of the whole system of fraud and inhumanity of slavery. It is so. The mode here adopted to disgust the slave with freedom, by allowing him to see only the abuse of it, is carried out in other things. For instance, a slave loves molasses; he steals some. His master, in many cases, goes off to town, and buys a large quantity; he returns, takes his whip, and commands the slave to eat the molasses, until the poor fellow is made sick at the very mention of it. The same mode is sometimes adopted to make the slaves refrain from asking for more food than their regular allowance. A slave runs through his allowance, and applies for more. His master is enraged at him; but, not willing to send him off without food, gives him more than is necessary, and compels him to eat it within a given time. Then, if he complains that he cannot eat it, he is said to be satisfied neither full nor fasting, and is whipped for being hard to please! I have an abundance of such illustrations of the same principle, drawn from my own observation, but think the cases I have cited sufficient. The practice is a very common one.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: The reader may consider me a hopeless busybody when I admit how much this man stimulated my curiosity and how often I tried to break through the reticence he showed concerning himself. Before passing judgment, however, one should remember how aimless my life was and how little there was to occupy my attention. My health prevented me from going out unless the weather was exceptionally mild, and I had no friends who would visit me and interrupt the monotony of my daily existence. Under these circumstances, I eagerly welcomed the small mystery surrounding my companion and spent much of my time attempting to unravel it.
output: The reader may set me down as a hopeless busybody, when I confess how much this man stimulated my curiosity, and how often I endeavoured to break through the reticence which he showed on all that concerned himself. Before pronouncing judgment, however, be it remembered, how objectless was my life, and how little there was to engage my attention. My health forbade me from venturing out unless the weather was exceptionally genial, and I had no friends who would call upon me and break the monotony of my daily existence. Under these circumstances, I eagerly hailed the little mystery which hung around my companion, and spent much of my time in endeavouring to unravel it.
title: A Study in Scarlet
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input: Jefferson Hope suggested that it may be advisable to start immediately, speaking in a calm yet determined tone that indicated his awareness of the serious danger they faced. He noted that while the front and back entrances are being monitored, it might be possible to escape through the side window and navigate across the fields with care.
