input: One night we captured a small section of a lumber raft, consisting of fine pine planks. It was twelve feet wide and approximately fifteen or sixteen feet long, and its surface stood six or seven inches above the water, forming a solid, level floor. Additionally, we could observe saw-logs drifting by during the daylight hours on occasion, but we allowed them to pass, as we did not reveal ourselves in daylight. Furthermore, on another night, while we were positioned near the head of the island just before daybreak, a frame house came floating down on the western side. It was a two-story structure and was tilted considerably. Moreover, we paddled out and boarded it, entering through an upstairs window. However, it was still too dark to see, so we secured the canoe and settled in it to await the arrival of daylight.
output:
One night we catched a little section of a lumber raft - nice pine planks. It was twelve foot wide and about fifteen or sixteen foot long, and the top stood above water six or seven inches - a solid, level floor. We could see saw-logs go by in the daylight sometimes, but we let them go; we didn’t show ourselves in daylight.

Another night when we was up at the head of the island, just before daylight, here comes a frame-house down, on the west side. She was a two-story, and tilted over considerable. We paddled out and got aboard - clumb in at an upstairs window. But it was too dark to see yet, so we made the canoe fast and set in her to wait for daylight.
title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain

input: As I made my way up the bank, I kept a watchful eye out for my father and also paid attention to what the rising water might bring. Before long, a canoe came into view, and it was a particularly nice one, approximately thirteen or fourteen feet in length, floating effortlessly on the water. I quickly jumped into the water, fully clothed, and swam out to the canoe, as I may have expected to find someone hiding in it, trying to trick people, but that was not the case this time. The canoe was indeed empty and had been drifting, so I climbed aboard and paddled it to the shore. I thought to myself that my father would likely be pleased when he saw the canoe, as it could be worth around ten dollars. However, when I reached the shore, my father was nowhere to be seen, and as I was guiding the canoe into a small, secluded creek surrounded by vines and willows, I had another idea: I decided it would be a good idea to hide the canoe and, instead of heading into the woods when I ran away, I could travel down the river by about fifty miles and set up camp in one location, which can often make for a more comfortable experience than constantly walking on foot. In summary, my discovery of the canoe led me to consider a new plan for when I would eventually run away.
output: I went along up the bank with one eye out for pap and t’other one out for what the rise might fetch along. Well, all at once here comes a canoe; just a beauty, too, about thirteen or fourteen foot long, riding high like a duck. I shot head-first off of the bank like a frog, clothes and all on, and struck out for the canoe. I just expected there’d be somebody laying down in it, because people often done that to fool folks, and when a chap had pulled a skiff out most to it they’d raise up and laugh at him. But it warn’t so this time. It was a drift-canoe sure enough, and I clumb in and paddled her ashore. Thinks I, the old man will be glad when he sees this - she’s worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore pap wasn’t in sight yet, and as I was running her into a little creek like a gully, all hung over with vines and willows, I struck another idea: I judged I’d hide her good, and then, ’stead of taking to the woods when I run off, I’d go down the river about fifty mile and camp in one place for good, and not have such a rough time tramping on foot.
title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain

input: A month or two ago, when Peter first fell ill, he expressed a sense of resignation about his recovery. He was quite old, and George's daughters were too young to provide him with much companionship, apart from Mary Jane, the red-haired girl. After George and his wife passed away, Peter felt increasingly lonely and showed little desire to continue living. He had a strong wish to see Harvey and William, as he was the type of person who could not bring himself to draft a will. He left behind a letter addressed to Harvey, in which he indicated the location of his hidden money and outlined how he wanted the rest of his property distributed, ensuring that George's daughters would be taken care of, since George had left them with nothing. That letter was the only document Peter was willing to write.
output: “Oh, yes; a month or two ago, when Peter was first took; because Peter said then that he sorter felt like he warn’t going to get well this time. You see, he was pretty old, and George’s g’yirls was too young to be much company for him, except Mary Jane, the red-headed one; and so he was kinder lonesome after George and his wife died, and didn’t seem to care much to live. He most desperately wanted to see Harvey - and William, too, for that matter - because he was one of them kind that can’t bear to make a will. He left a letter behind for Harvey, and said he’d told in it where his money was hid, and how he wanted the rest of the property divided up so George’s g’yirls would be all right - for George didn’t leave nothing. And that letter was all they could get him to put a pen to.”
title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain

input: I had spent quite some time on the ground, crawling out of the hole and removing various items. To address this, I made some improvements from the outside by spreading dust over the area, which helped to disguise the smooth surface and the sawdust. I then returned the piece of log to its original position, securing it with two rocks underneath and one against it to keep it stable, as it was slightly raised at that spot and did not quite rest on the ground. If someone were to stand four or five feet away and was unaware that it had been sawed, they might not notice anything unusual. Furthermore, this was the back of the cabin, so it was unlikely that anyone would be exploring that area. In summary, my efforts may have effectively concealed the repairs I made.
output: I had wore the ground a good deal crawling out of the hole and dragging out so many things. So I fixed that as good as I could from the outside by scattering dust on the place, which covered up the smoothness and the sawdust. Then I fixed the piece of log back into its place, and put two rocks under it and one against it to hold it there, for it was bent up at that place and didn’t quite touch ground. If you stood four or five foot away and didn’t know it was sawed, you wouldn’t never notice it; and besides, this was the back of the cabin, and it warn’t likely anybody would go fooling around there.
title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain

input:
Laws knows that I may have wanted to visit Tom badly enough to consider going, and I had every intention to do so; however, after a certain point, I really wouldn’t have gone, even for great rewards. 

Yet, both she and Tom occupied my thoughts, leading to a rather restless night. I found myself wandering down the path twice during the night, quietly approaching the front. Each time, I noticed her sitting by the candle in the window, gazing down the road with tears in her eyes. I wished I could do something to help her, but I felt powerless, aside from promising myself that I would never again do anything to upset her. When I awoke at dawn for the third time and slipped back down, she was still there. Her candle was nearly extinguished, and her head was resting on her hand as she slept. In summary, my concern for her and my determination to avoid causing her distress were strong throughout the night.
output:
Laws knows I wanted to go bad enough to see about Tom, and was all intending to go; but after that I wouldn’t a went, not for kingdoms.

But she was on my mind and Tom was on my mind, so I slept very restless. And twice I went down the rod away in the night, and slipped around front, and see her setting there by her candle in the window with her eyes towards the road and the tears in them; and I wished I could do something for her, but I couldn’t, only to swear that I wouldn’t never do nothing to grieve her any more. And the third time I waked up at dawn, and slid down, and she was there yet, and her candle was most out, and her old gray head was resting on her hand, and she was asleep.
title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain

input:
The man approached and pushed the chair on which Linton sat. He should have maintained his distance. My master quickly stood up and struck him forcefully on the throat, a blow that would have incapacitated a weaker individual. The impact took the man's breath away for a moment. While he choked, Mr. Linton exited through the back door and made his way to the front entrance.

“He is not coming,” I said, crafting a small deception. “There are the coachman and the two gardeners. You will not want to be thrown into the road by them. Each one carries a club, and the master will likely be watching from the parlor windows to ensure they follow his orders.”
output:
The fellow approached and gave the chair on which Linton rested a push. He’d better have kept his distance: my master quickly sprang erect, and struck him full on the throat a blow that would have levelled a slighter man. It took his breath for a minute; and while he choked, Mr. Linton walked out by the back door into the yard, and from thence to the front entrance.

“He is not coming,” I interposed, framing a bit of a lie. “There’s the coachman and the two gardeners; you’ll surely not wait to be thrust into the road by them! Each has a bludgeon; and master will, very likely, be watching from the parlour-windows to see that they fulfil his orders.”
title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë

input:
“Here and here,” replied Catherine, as she struck one hand against her forehead and the other against her breast. “In whichever place the soul resides, I am convinced in both my soul and my heart that I am in error.” 

She settled herself beside me once more; her expression became increasingly somber and serious, and her clasped hands began to tremble. 

“Oh, do not, Miss Catherine!” I exclaimed. “We are already dismal enough without summoning ghosts and visions to trouble us. Come, let us be joyful and true to yourself! Observe little Hareton; he is not dreaming of anything gloomy. How sweetly he smiles in his sleep!”
output:
“Here! and here!” replied Catherine, striking one hand on her forehead, and the other on her breast: “in whichever place the soul lives. In my soul and in my heart, I’m convinced I’m wrong!”

She seated herself by me again: her countenance grew sadder and graver, and her clasped hands trembled.

“Oh! don’t, Miss Catherine!” I cried. “We’re dismal enough without conjuring up ghosts and visions to perplex us. Come, come, be merry and like yourself! Look at little Hareton! he’s dreaming nothing dreary. How sweetly he smiles in his sleep!”
title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë

input: Yes, if we can keep him, I thought to myself, though I had serious doubts that there was much hope of it. I then wondered how such a weak child could possibly live at Wuthering Heights, with his father and Hareton as his companions and teachers. Our uncertainty was soon resolved, even sooner than I expected. I had just taken the children upstairs after tea and had seen Linton fall asleep—he would not let me leave until he was asleep—when I came back down and was standing by the table in the hall, lighting a bedroom candle for Mr. Edgar. At that moment, a maid came out of the kitchen and told me that Mr. Heathcliff’s servant Joseph was at the door and wished to speak with the master.
output: “Ay, if we can keep him!” I mused to myself; and sore misgivings came over me that there was slight hope of that. And then, I thought, how ever will that weakling live at Wuthering Heights? Between his father and Hareton, what playmates and instructors they’ll be. Our doubts were presently decided - even earlier than I expected. I had just taken the children upstairs, after tea was finished, and seen Linton asleep - he would not suffer me to leave him till that was the case - I had come down, and was standing by the table in the hall, lighting a bedroom candle for Mr. Edgar, when a maid stepped out of the kitchen and informed me that Mr. Heathcliff’s servant Joseph was at the door, and wished to speak with the master.
title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë

input: The speaker advocates for allowing Catherine to remain in her current location while suggesting that Master Linton be sent to her. They argue that since the listener has negative feelings toward both individuals, their absence would not be felt and that their presence serves as a burden. The listener responds by stating their intention to find a tenant for the Grange and expresses a desire to keep their children close. They also assert that Catherine is indebted to them for her livelihood and that they will not support her in a life of comfort and inactivity after Linton leaves. The conversation concludes with a demand for prompt action and a warning against the need for coercion.
output:
“Why not let Catherine continue here,” I pleaded, “and send Master Linton to her? As you hate them both, you’d not miss them: they can only be a daily plague to your unnatural heart.”

“I’m seeking a tenant for the Grange,” he answered; “and I want my children about me, to be sure. Besides, that lass owes me her services for her bread. I’m not going to nurture her in luxury and idleness after Linton is gone. Make haste and get ready, now; and don’t oblige me to compel you.”
title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë

input:
I stirred up the cinders and then fetched a scuttleful of coal. The invalid was complaining about being covered in ashes, however, he was also experiencing a persistent cough and appeared to be feverish and unwell, so I did not reprimand him for his behavior. 

He inquired as to why I had not arrived sooner, and he suggested that I should have come to visit instead of sending a letter. He noted that writing the long letters had been extremely tiring for him, and he would have preferred to have a conversation with me. At this point, he was feeling too unwell to engage in conversation or any other activity. Additionally, he was wondering about the whereabouts of Zillah, and he asked me if I would be willing to step into the kitchen to see if she was there.
output:
I stirred up the cinders, and fetched a scuttleful myself. The invalid complained of being covered with ashes; but he had a tiresome cough, and looked feverish and ill, so I did not rebuke his temper.

“Why didn’t you come before?” he asked. “You should have come, instead of writing. It tired me dreadfully writing those long letters. I’d far rather have talked to you. Now, I can neither bear to talk, nor anything else. I wonder where Zillah is! Will you” (looking at me) “step into the kitchen and see?”
title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë

input: He exclaimed that it was fortunate they were out of his reach, and demanded to know what compelled Hareton to continually stare at him with an unrelenting gaze. He ordered Hareton to look away and not remind him of his presence again, adding that he had thought he had put an end to Hareton's laughter. This highlights the tense dynamic between the two individuals. Hareton chose not to respond, instead focusing on his plate. Mr. Heathcliff briefly looked at him before returning to his breakfast and his thoughts. Ultimately, the rest of the meal proceeded without incident, as the two young people distanced themselves from each other. This suggests that they were attempting to avoid further conflict. Just as we were finishing, Joseph appeared at the door, his quivering lip and furious eyes indicating that he had discovered the damage done to his prized shrubs. It is likely that he had seen Cathy and her cousin near the affected area before inspecting it, as he began to speak in a manner that was difficult to understand due to his agitation, his jaws working in a way that resembled a cow chewing its cud.
output:
“It is well you are out of my reach,” he exclaimed. “What fiend possesses you to stare back at me, continually, with those infernal eyes? Down with them! and don’t remind me of your existence again. I thought I had cured you of laughing.”

Hareton looked at his plate, and did not repeat the confession. Mr. Heathcliff looked at him a bit, and then silently resumed his breakfast and his interrupted musing. We had nearly finished, and the two young people prudently shifted wider asunder, so I anticipated no further disturbance during that sitting: when Joseph appeared at the door, revealing by his quivering lip and furious eyes that the outrage committed on his precious shrubs was detected. He must have seen Cathy and her cousin about the spot before he examined it, for while his jaws worked like those of a cow chewing its cud, and rendered his speech difficult to understand, he began: -
title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë

input: The old woman responded, "Regarding the gentleman in question, it may be beneficial for you to consider the potential consequences of your actions, as it's possible that things could become difficult for you. Nevertheless, that's not my concern; my role is to care for you and help you recover, which I will do to the best of my ability while maintaining a clear conscience - it would be beneficial if everyone could do the same. I turned away from the woman, feeling a sense of distaste towards her seemingly insensitive remarks, especially given my fragile state at the time. However, I was also feeling rather weak and struggled to process everything that had happened. My life experiences seemed somewhat surreal, and I can often find myself wondering if they actually occurred, as they tend to lack a sense of realism when I think back on them. In summary, the old woman's words had a profound impact on me, and I was left feeling uncertain and disconnected from my past.
output:
“For that matter,” replied the old woman, “if you mean about the gentleman you murdered, I believe that it were better for you if you were dead, for I fancy it will go hard with you! However, that’s none of my business; I am sent to nurse you and get you well; I do my duty with a safe conscience; it were well if everybody did the same.”

I turned with loathing from the woman who could utter so unfeeling a speech to a person just saved, on the very edge of death; but I felt languid and unable to reflect on all that had passed. The whole series of my life appeared to me as a dream; I sometimes doubted if indeed it were all true, for it never presented itself to my mind with the force of reality.
title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley

input: As I looked up, I saw the demon standing at the window, illuminated by the light of the moon. This sight caused me to tremble and my heart to fail within me. The demon's face was distorted by a gruesome smile as he stared at me, seated and engaged in the task that he had assigned to me. Meanwhile, it became clear that he had been following me throughout my travels. He had been lurking in forests, concealing himself in caves, and seeking refuge in vast and isolated areas of wilderness. Furthermore, he had now appeared to monitor my progress and demand that I fulfill the promise that I had made to him.
output: I trembled and my heart failed within me, when, on looking up, I saw by the light of the moon the dæmon at the casement. A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he gazed on me, where I sat fulfilling the task which he had allotted to me. Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress and claim the fulfilment of my promise.
title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley

input: While I was engaged in repairing the boat and organizing the sails, a group of individuals gathered nearby. They appeared surprised by my presence, but instead of providing help, they whispered to one another and gestured in a manner that could have caused concern under different circumstances. However, I noted that they were speaking English and chose to communicate with them in that language. I asked, "Could you please tell me the name of this town and where I am?"
output: As I was occupied in fixing the boat and arranging the sails, several people crowded towards the spot. They seemed much surprised at my appearance, but instead of offering me any assistance, whispered together with gestures that at any other time might have produced in me a slight sensation of alarm. As it was, I merely remarked that they spoke English, and I therefore addressed them in that language. “My good friends,” said I, “will you be so kind as to tell me the name of this town and inform me where I am?”
title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley

input: The lion settled onto his back on a sofa beside the drinking table, while the jackal occupied his own cluttered table on the opposite side, equipped with bottles and glasses. Both engaged in drinking, but their approaches differed significantly. The lion lounged with his hands resting in his waistband, gazing at the fire or occasionally perusing lighter materials. In contrast, the jackal focused intently on his work, his brow furrowed, so immersed that he often struggled to find his glass, sometimes searching for over a minute before successfully locating it. Occasionally, the complexity of his task compelled the jackal to rise and refresh his towels. Upon returning from these trips to the jug and basin, he donned unusual and damp headgear, which appeared even more absurd given his serious demeanor. This highlights the contrasting behaviors of the two characters, reflecting their differing personalities and approaches to their task.
output: The lion then composed himself on his back on a sofa on one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal sat at his own paper-bestrewn table proper, on the other side of it, with the bottles and glasses ready to his hand. Both resorted to the drinking-table without stint, but each in a different way; the lion for the most part reclining with his hands in his waistband, looking at the fire, or occasionally flirting with some lighter document; the jackal, with knitted brows and intent face, so deep in his task, that his eyes did not even follow the hand he stretched out for his glass - which often groped about, for a minute or more, before it found the glass for his lips. Two or three times, the matter in hand became so knotty, that the jackal found it imperative on him to get up, and steep his towels anew. From these pilgrimages to the jug and basin, he returned with such eccentricities of damp headgear as no words can describe; which were made the more ludicrous by his anxious gravity.
title: A Tale of Two Cities
author: Charles Dickens

input: The speaker expresses deep regret for causing a situation and requests someone to convey their sincere apologies to another person. Mr. Carton displays a careless demeanor, bordering on insolence, as he leans against the bar, partially turned away from the prisoner. He suggests that expecting a certain outcome is wise and likely, but also indicates that their withdrawal may actually benefit the situation. Jerry, unable to linger outside the courtroom, departs without hearing further conversation. He observes the two individuals standing side by side, noting that while they share similar features, their manners are quite different, as reflected in the glass above them.
output:
“I am deeply sorry to have been the cause of it. Could you tell her so for me, with my fervent acknowledgments?”

Mr. Carton’s manner was so careless as to be almost insolent. He stood, half turned from the prisoner, lounging with his elbow against the bar.

“It’s the wisest thing to expect, and the likeliest. But I think their withdrawing is in your favour.”

Loitering on the way out of court not being allowed, Jerry heard no more: but left them - so like each other in feature, so unlike each other in manner - standing side by side, both reflected in the glass above them.
title: A Tale of Two Cities
author: Charles Dickens

input:
He gazed at her with a fearful expression, and after a moment, his lips began to form words, although no sound was audible. As he paused between breaths, which were rapid and labored, he was eventually heard to speak.

Meanwhile, tears streamed down her face, and she brought her hands to her lips, kissing them as a gesture to him. Subsequently, she clasped her hands to her breast, as if she were cradling his injured head.

She did not yet trust her voice, so she sat down beside him on the bench. However, he recoiled from her, but she gently placed her hand on his arm. This action caused a strange sensation to pass through him, which was visible in his physical reaction. Consequently, he laid the knife down quietly, continuing to stare at her.
output:
He stared at her with a fearful look, and after a while his lips began to form some words, though no sound proceeded from them. By degrees, in the pauses of his quick and laboured breathing, he was heard to say:

With the tears streaming down her face, she put her two hands to her lips, and kissed them to him; then clasped them on her breast, as if she laid his ruined head there.

Not yet trusting the tones of her voice, she sat down on the bench beside him. He recoiled, but she laid her hand upon his arm. A strange thrill struck him when she did so, and visibly passed over his frame; he laid the knife down softly, as he sat staring at her.
title: A Tale of Two Cities
author: Charles Dickens
